On clause 1-Part I.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE PAYMENT OF DEATH BENEFITS UP TO MAXIMUM OF $5,000
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to make an extended statement about this bill because, as hon. members are aware, it was considered by the committee on banking and commerce. I was not present at the hearings of that committee but I understand the main subject matter discussed there was whether or not the bill should be dealt with at this time, or should be postponed. It is on that point I wish to say a word.
As I said in my speech on second reading, this is a bill which, in the view of the government, rounds out the superannuation act, an act which in my opinion is one of the best, if not the best, superannuation plans offered by any employer in Canada. Those of us who have had some legal experience-and that covers a good many of us-know that unfortunately a good many people do not make adequate provision for the liabilities they leave at death. We see a good many hard cases where provision of some additional liquid resources would prove greatly advantageous either to the dependents of the deceased or to those who are responsible for discharging the obligations.
This measure was given very careful consideration by the government before it was decided to introduce it. It is, of course, a compulsory plan. Any plan of this sort must be compulsory in order that the benefits of the low rate may be available. My understanding is that the superintendent of insurance gave evidence to that effect before the committee.
I think it is unlikely that there could be any substantial variation in the plan as presented. In other words, I think the plan must be taken as a whole. It is true that you could, for instance, exclude women from its operation. But I am one who does not believe that women should be discriminated against in matters of this kind. I can see no reason why they should be excluded. They would have to be excluded as a whole; you could not exclude unmarried women and include married women, and so on.
In the case of similar plans, I may say that they are compulsory and are made applicable to everybody. For instance, the plan in the Bank of Canada applies from the lowliest stenographer to the most senior executive. The same applies to the plan in force in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It has been suggested that we ought to put this over for further consideration. Well, I am not one who believes that a plan of this kind, which has been carefully

considered by the actuaries and by the technical people who studied its soundness, would be benefited by a postponement. I think the committee should bear in mind that, as I am told, something over 400 civil servants die each year, and that if this plan is postponed for a year-as I understand has been suggested-it becomes quite clear that the dependents would lose the benefit of the provisions of this measure.
For the price of four or five packages of cigarettes a month a civil servant can provide a liquid amount of up to $5,000 to discharge the obligations he leaves behind him upon his death. So far as I am concerned, I think it is an excellent plan. As I have said elsewhere, I only wish I were eligible to participate in it.
For reasons, some of which I have indicated, the government can see no good reason for postponing this plan.

Speaking of the desire on the part of the civil servants for further consultation he says: "I am not one of those who believes that a plan which has been carefully considered by the government", and so on-I did not get the exact words-but in effect they were "needs further consideration."

speechtext:
I am grateful for the implied compliment. One often wonders whether one is worth hearing. I was assured the other day that I very seldom am because I am always wrong. However, a man who is wrong can be useful in strengthening other people's views.
The minister has put his finger at once on one of the main points I want to emphasize. We have a situation here where more than 200,000 of our fellow civil servants, without anything approaching what may be called consultation, are being dragooned into a scheme which it is perfectly clear from the evidence already available, fragmentary as it is by reason of the short time, many of them are against. As a matter of fact, if on May 26, when this bill was introduced, anyone had predicted to me that the situation we find this morning could have arisen I could hardly have believed it.
What is the situation as we sit here this morning? On May 26 the bill was introduced. On May 27 the banking and commerce committee met, and the energetic and expeditious chairman told us that the various civil service
14. 1954
Public Service Superannuation Act organizations would be coming before us, and he gave us their names. He said that they were not prepared to make representations that morning. That was not a very surprising statement considering that they represent large groups-one represents something like 60,000 civil servants-from end to end of Canada, and they all have wide dispersion of their membership. But the chairman said, perhaps with a little unconscious humour-no, not unconscious, the chairman always has his sense of humour with him-"in order that they should be given ample opportunity we will call our next meeting on Wednesday afternoon." That was, I think, six days later. Ample opportunity to discuss with tens of thousands of members across Canada a complicated measure running into 30 or 40 clauses!
It is true the bill had been discussed after a fashion with what is called the national joint council. The minister seemed to think that the national joint council consultation had carried the matter a considerable distance; but from the evidence before us it would appear that there is very little to that point, and I shall come to it in a moment or two.
There are two points that I wish to emphasize. First of all there has been no proper discussion with those concerned. Second, there is an element of compulsion which was unanimously objected to by the representatives that came before us. We of the opposition discussed this in the committee at some length and moved that the bill be not reported on the ground that all civil servants' representatives asked for further opportunity to discuss it, and that it was a reasonable request. That motion was dealt with in less time than it takes to tell it. No answer was given to the arguments, such as they were. The chairman merely put it to a vote, and you will not be surprised, Mr. Chairman, to know what the result of the vote was.
This bill purports to benefit civil servants, and if we in the opposition thought it was calculated to do this with a maximum of justice or with even a minimum of injustice we would be wholeheartedly for it.

Nor can I discover from the evidence that it purports to do so. It was a mere conduit pipe which received information. If it had been able to pass on the information it received then it would have been discharging a useful function; but it was bound over to secrecy, and since then there has been, as I shall point out later from briefs presented to the committee, widespread complaint which I shall go into more in detail.
The government is forcing the matter through, though they know there is widespread disapproval. They cannot know how widespread it is because there has been no time. For example, one of the organizations that came before us had 80 branches. Immediately the information was available to them they had communicated with the 80 branches, but they had had time to hear from only 5. Seventy-five have not yet been heard from. Incidentally, evidence was given to us that in one case a week was required; in other cases a good deal longer. In any event, of course they could have got the full report if there had been time. I shall quote later from the briefs to point out the extent of the disapproval.
Actually, when I saw those briefs I said: "Well, the party is over; the government will never go ahead immediately in the face of this; they will at least consult with these people." I could hardly believe my ears when this thing was rammed through the committee. As I say, they did not deign even to answer the arguments that were made. That was not flattering, but I think we knew the reason. The reason was that there was to be no opportunity for discussion. The word was that it was to be forced through; it had to go back by such and such a day. I think the chairman of the committee had precious little discretion in the matter.
I want to quote a little later on at some length from the briefs. I am not going to go into the details of the many recommendations made. I am going to dwell wholly on the two chief points, the points which I think should have moved the government to delay. The first of them is the universal feeling that there should have been further
[Mr. Macdonnell.l

consultation. The second was the universal feeling that the objections to compulsion were already strong, and evidence to indicate it was likely to be just as strong when the full reports were in.
In introducing the bill the minister said, as reported at page 5103 of Hansard:
-I can inform the house that the national joint council has endorsed the broad outlines of the plan as a whole.
Well, I have not found that impressive. It might have been impressive if in fact this national joint council had had any authority and still more if this national joint council had been able to pass on the information that it got, which indeed it got months ago. But in fact this national joint council, as I shall point out, has no authority and did not pretend to have. Mr. Johnston representing the civil service association of Ottawa says:
The national joint council . . . was not in a position to make any endorsation of the plan, as most of the staff side representatives were only able to express their views as individuals.
And again he says:
This proposal was presented to the council in a very unusual way, which involved the strictest secrecy on the part of all members of the council. The staff side were unable to deal with this subject in their normal way, by taking it back to their associations for guidance.
One would not only regard that as the normal way; one would regard it as a very reasonable way. Indeed it is the only way in which sensible people should deal with each other.
There were two courses open to the government. One was the natural, effective, normal, almost inevitable course for reasonable men, and that was to carry through effective consultation in the ordinary way, which they have often done before, with these civil service organizations which are serious representatives of the civil servants. Among them they represent, I should think, well over 62,000 out of the more than 100,000 civil servant involved.
Now, at the other extreme, there was another course no reasonable man would recommend but which might have been logical, namely, to have no consultation of any kind but just to ram it through and care nothing for what anyone said. As I said, that would have been to me wholly unreasonable. I suppose you can be logical and at the same time utterly unreasonable. But at any rate neither course was followed. A middle course, which had the worst of both elements in it, which was neither one thing nor the other, was followed. The government made a show of consultation by talking to the national joint council but it made this procedure wholly useless by imposing secrecy

on them. In other words, there was just a pretence or a show of consultation which meant not a thing in the world.
As I shall show later, when the bill became public most of the civil service organizations reported widespread disapproval of the vital details. Every organization wanted more time for consultation and every organization raised complaints about the compulsory feature of the bill. Now, we in the opposition are I suppose rather old-fashioned people, but we have the idea that consultation would be natural, particularly if you are placing burdens on people. After all, it is not as if the government was coming along with a Christmas present.
Even one week of consultation showed so much opposition that it seems to me it is utterly preposterous for the government to force this measure through. The only motto I can think of which motivates the government is, "treat them rough and tell them nothing". That, I believe, was a recipe once given for dealing with a man's wife but I do not think it should be extended to more human relationships.
Indeed, we argued these points and we asked for delay. We moved that the committee do not report the bill, but we were voted down. We are used to that, of course, but it would have been nice to have some reasons. Mr. Chairman, we would have felt that perhaps we were discharging our duty better if the government had felt it worth while even to give us some reason. As I say, they are placing burdens on these people and there is no reason why they should just shove it through. But the government pays no attention to the request of tens of thousands of civil servants who ask for a chance to be heard.
Well, Mr. Chairman, one wonders whether ordinary decent human relationships should not prevail in relation to civil servants. No one can deny that this bill works hardship on them. The minister will not deny that and his answer is that in order to be effective the bill has got to be compulsory.

speechtext:
A very large number die after reaching 70 and will obtain no benefit at all. There is widespread evidence and nothing to discount the evidence that the unmarried woman, and indeed other women, are very much opposed to this. Are they not entitled to be heard? As I say, one can only assume that the government is prepared to ram the bill through regardless of any injustice involved.
Now I come to the armed forces. There was an attempt made to consult the armed forces but some of us have been in the armed forces and we regard consultation within the armed forces much as would a man from Missouri. When we learned that consultation had been held and a few area commanders were able to report back that the majority of the soldiers were in favour of the scheme I argued quite strongly in committee that I just could not conceive that any man of 17 or 18 years of age, who enlisted for three years, would be in favour of this. He would probably know of his own knowledge that the average enlistment is about five years-out of the 25,000 annual enlistment there is an average wastage of 16,000. I argued that it was impossible to believe that if that young man had it made clear to him, first of all, that when he left the service, unless he elected to continue as a member of the plan and pay his subscription for the rest of his life, perhaps for 40 years, he would lose money, he would lose all benefit. It is impossible for me to conceive that such a man would be in favour of this thing. The answer was made, "Well, of course, he likes it because of the combat feature." But there is a Pension Act and I think that if that young man, as regards the combat feature, had been reminded of the rights of his dependents or relatives under the Pension Act it is just not conceivable that he would have been in favour of it. Yet, we are asked to believe that many were in favour.
Now, coming back to the question of consultation with the civil servants I want to read a word again from Mr. Johnston who spoke on behalf of the association:
The procedure followed by the government . . . was, in my opinion, an indication that the government lacked confidence in its employees and their associations to handle a subject of this nature.
This bill, Mr. Chairman, got lost. It should never have come here at all. It should have

Public Service Superannuation Act been used merely as a basis for discussion with those whom it was contemplated to benefit.
How does good legislation arise? Does it arise in this shotgun manner? Or does it arise by a much better and more judicious procedure? I will quote the minister against himself, and on this point I refer to the Bank Act. Was that brought before us in this shotgun manner? No! The minister took pains to give a hearing to those who would validly be asked to express their views. The minister attended some meetings, took the time to answer questions, and showed the greatest interest in the matter. After weeks, and indeed months, of careful discussion the committee report was brought down. Again when there was a complete revision of income tax some years ago I very well remember the trouble the minister took to communicate with all sorts of organizations.
Now, is this measure so unimportant? It involves 200,000 people. Was there no reason that this should have been discussed? Why should the civil servants and members of the armed forces be treated in this fashion? The only answer I can give when I look at the minister's action here and compare it in the other cases is that when a good man goes wrong he is most dangerous because he remembers the times when he was right and he becomes just as stubborn in the wrong as he previously was in the right. At any rate, though the minister had this consultation with the national joint council it really was utterly meaningless because he bound them over to secrecy, and there was no proper and adequate consultation with the representatives of those involved.
This bill puts a burden on civil servants in many cases while giving them no opportunity to be heard. Many will pay for years and receive no money back. If a private employer did things in this fashion there would be an outcry. Would it not have been fairer to assemble certain facts-for example to find out how many are carrying as much insurance as they think they can under the present Civil Service Insurance Act and otherwise; to find out how many women regard this procedure as a star chamber imposition, not for their benefit but for the benefit of others whom the government has selected as the objects of their benevolence. Would it not have been better to find out in a real way the attitude of the men in the forces? Let us take one small suggestion that came out. I do not propose to refer to it at length, but it struck me as common sense having regard to what the minister said when introducing the bill. He described it, in a manner of

speaking, as a kind of burial measure. I notice that one of the representatives suggested that if it was a burial measure, perhaps $1,000 would be enough with which to get buried.
As I listen to my own words, inadequate as they are-200,000 people being dragooned in this fashion; it sounds almost incredible to me that it should be so-I ask myself, am I unfair? To answer that question I shall quote from these briefs at some little length. I shall be as brief as I can, but I think it is essential that these things should be on the record.
First of all, as to the matter of consultation, I read from the brief of the Civil Service Federation of Canada:
The various staff associations affiliated with the Civil Service Federation of Canada protest strongly the fact that they were not given an opportunity to study the plan before the bill was introduced.
That is plain enough. Then I come to the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada. They say as follows:
However, in the matter of death benefits, and not to labour the point, no organization on the national joint council had authority to either consult national executives or membership until Wednesday, May 26th. On which day the second reading of the bill was given in the House of Commons. From that date to this being far too short a time to afford proper consultation.
I will say that it was too short a time. They continue:
Therefore, in consulting the national joint council some twenty individual views were obtained by the government. It being clearly understood that no staff-side representative could be considered as speaking for his or her organization.
I now come to the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada which says this:
The professional institute regrets that the public service was not asked beforehand for an expression of the opinion of a good cross section of all units on the radical departures involved in this plan as the armed forces were.
They were optimistic in thinking that the armed forces were asked. The brief continues:
In effect the preliminary negotiations for this scheme took the form of consultation with members of the national joint council and one of its subcommittees as individuals only, not as representatives of their organizations. Consequently, the view of the institute is that the public service was not given an opportunity to consider the proposed plan before Tuesday, 25 May 1954.
Then I come to the Civil Service Association of Ottawa which says this. They refer to what Mr. Taylor had said on Thursday last and state:
It is my understanding that the national joint council, as an employer-employee council, was not in a position to make any endorsation of the plan, as most of the staff side representatives were only able to express their views as individuals. This

proposal was presented to the council in a very unusual way, which involved the strictest secrecy on the part of all members of the council. The staff side were unable to deal with this subject in their normal way, by taking it back to their associations for guidance. The staff side cannot function as part of the council unless the association representatives can speak on behalf of their associations. And unless the staff side is allowed to proceed in this way, the council itself cannot function as an employer-employee body.
The procedure followed by the government in only allowing the members of the council to make personal suggestions on the plan presented to them was, in my opinion, an indication that the government lacked confidence in its employees and their associations to handle a subject of this nature.
Last I come to the comment of the Department of Veterans Affairs organization which says this:
We feel strongly that any bill concerning the entire body of civil servants should be brought to the attention of that body before such legislation is introduced in the House of Commons.
They feel that strongly, and any sensible person should feel it strongly. I come now to the compulsion side and I read from the brief of the Civil Service Federation:
It is recommended that civil servants be given the option as to whether they contribute in accordance with the amount of their salary or up to $3,000, say, to a grade 4 level; and on the amount of their salary or $5,000 above that level.
And again at page 2:
It is recommended that the compulsory feature of the act in regard to employees having reached age 60 be changed to give them the right to elect for participation;-
Then I read from the brief of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada:
I am in no position today to support the bill in all its aspects. From a sampling of opinion received to date, however, it appears that the principle of the bill is widely acceptable. On the other hand, opposition is developing to the compulsory feature. In evidence of this I would cite a telegram received from our Vancouver local council, a council with a membership of close to one thousand.
"Vancouver local council agree in principle to life insurance (death benefits) scheme but protest compulsory clauses-"
Again at page 2 of the brief of the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada:
I would, therefore, on behalf of my organization very strongly and heartily support the principle of the bill, and in this also express to the government our appreciation. On the other hand, I must just as strongly oppose the compulsory features of the bill, and request the same be amended so as to provide that the plan become elective.
Then the professional institute at page 3 of their brief say:
The compulsory nature of the proposed scheme is objected to by a number of individual public servants. It is felt that they have certain rights as individuals, irrespective of what the majority view might be. The large number of public servants who will benefit from the scheme are not entitled to enjoy unusually low premium rates if these rates are based on compulsion applied to individuals who would prefer not to be insured.

The Ottawa association at page 8 of their brief say this:
-and that further consideration be given to the universal, compulsory feature of the present bill.
In the light of these quotations, Mr. Chairman, is it any wonder that strong objection is taken to the compulsory nature of the bill by the veterans affairs organization? They comment on the compulsory feature as follows:
The majority of us are very gravely concerned with the arbitrariness of the legislation . . . Such disregard of the will of the people seems to bear the taint of authoritarian paternalism . . .
Yet the government goes on from one arbitrariness to another. I have already referred to the fact only a fraction of the civil service could be communicated with in the time available. I have pointed out the extraordinary unanimity and forcefulness of their objections on the two counts that I have stressed. Yet the government goes on. When there was some apparent delay last week I had hoped that it might be possible that the arguments put forward in the committee had had some weight. But if indeed there ever was any thought of adopting a reasonable course, it has evidently been put aside. I can only urge the government that even yet they adopt a course which, 1 submit, would be reasonable and natural and, indeed, with a good employer, inevitable.
I urge them to deal with their employees as responsible men and women. As I said earlier, why should the civil servants be singled out for this kind of treatment? Are they not responsible people? Are they not people whom we all respect? I said in the committee when I opposed the reporting of the bill that if it were reported in its then form it would be reported utterly regardless of the weight of evidence before the committee, and I can only hope that this committee will consider the weight of evidence and will not follow the course taken by the banking and commerce committee.

Whether it will be extended to make it available to people outside the civil service. The minister shakes his head, but my question makes the point, namely, that there are people who will not have the advantage of this plan who see it as a very good one. As I say, I wish there had been an attempt made before the legislation was brought in to sell the good points of the plan to the civil servants.
A good deal is being said about its compulsory feature. I notice that if you are opposed to the plan you call it a compulsory plan and if you are for it you call it a universal plan. The two words mean the same thing, in the end. But the minister this morning, and others who have spoken on the legislation previously, have pointed out that the only possibility of any scheme of insurance being provided at low rates arises when you have what we call universal coverage. Something more on that basic principle will be heard from us before the week is out, certainly before the session ends, with regard to the desirability of a national health insurance program.
I think too that an educational job might have been done and may well yet have to be done with regard to the nature of the protection that is afforded by the plan. People are confused about insurance. I do not think that insurance agents are to blame for all that confusion but they certainly help to create it by trying to sell people these policies under which they are supposed to win either way. People do not realize that in any kind of insurance that affords protection there is a certain part of the cost which is the cost of the protection, and if you do not die within the period in which you are protected that element which covered the


cost of protection is, to use a colloquial term, "down the drain". What people do not realize is that if you outlive the period for which the protection was provided and thereby do not get your money back, you have not lost, you have won. You have won in the sense that you are still alive.
As I say, I think a more useful job might have been done by way of educating civil servants as to the nature of the protection that is being afforded by this plan and as to the exceptionally low rates that the civil servants are getting. As I say, we wish there could have been consultation in advance, and we hope that even yet a greater job of educating civil servants as to the nature of the plan will be done. But even so that does not detract from the fact that this is a very beneficial and advantageous offer that is being made by the government to our civil servants.
A number of things came out in the committee that interested me. I think it is splendid the way in which the $5,000 ceiling applies even in the case of persons who might now get as much as $2,500 by way of the two months' death benefit if they are in a high bracket, whereas those a little lower down will get a greater advantage if they die while in service. I think too that the right afforded to a civil servant who has been in the service for five years to take the insurance with him and carry it for the rest of the allotted time, if he wishes to do so, is a good idea. In view of that, I do not think it is so terribly farfetched for me to ask my question whether a plan like this might be made available to the people of Canada generally. In closing I can sum up the way we feel about this measure by saying that I have run across a good many people who will not be able to qualify for this protection because they are not civil servants who wish that this plan could be made available to them.

The ministry of finance is certainly not a portfolio in which one is trained in idealism,

I was speaking of the features of the bill. I said the first one was the compulsory feature. In the second place we are asked to apply it to all personnel of the service and all personnel of the forces.
The third feature is that the benefits are of a very limited nature. That is something that I think has escaped adequate appreciation in the way the government has put this before us or has discussed it at another time.
These are extremely limited benefits. There is nothing provided except a death benefit. It is the barest kind of insurance, the barest you can imagine. There is no secret about that, and we well know that when the civil servant passes the age of sixty and enters his declining years the benefits begin to undergo reduction as well, and by the time he has reached the age of seventy there is no insurance left, none whatever.
Let us recognize at once, Mr. Chairman, that this is not the ordinary kind of group term insurance with which many hon. members are familiar. Let us look a little further at the attempts that have been made to compare this scheme with existing schemes of group insurance. The fact of the matter is that there is no fair basis of comparison of this scheme with any existing scheme.
Now, we had some curious assertions on the part of Liberal members in that committee. The hon. member for Vancouver South unburdened himself of the authoritative assertion that this was the kind of insurance which if written through some private organization would cost 80 cents per thousand per month, or double the figure named in the bill. Well, I hope the hon. member has learned the error of his ways because the facts were put before the committee by Mr. MacGregor, superintendent of insurance. Mr. MacGregor disposed completely of nonsense of that kind. He drew attention in the first place to the fact that the largest group covered by any system of group insurance in Canada written


hitherto is 15,000. The group proposed by this measure numbers 230,000, more than 15 times the size of any existing group covered by a group insurance scheme in Canada and, as Mr. MacGregor pointed out, this is of a different order entirely. I would refer members to what he said at page 1736 of the evidence when, comparing this scheme with any other existing scheme, he said it was extremely difficult to make any valid comparison and, comparing this scheme with any other group insurance scheme in existence, he said it was of a different order entirely.
Mr. MacGregor pointed out as well that the cost of a scheme would be governed, broadly speaking, in inverse relationship to the size of the group. Here you have a group 15 times the size of the maximum group under any existing group insurance scheme in Canada today. If the cost moved down with the upward extension of the group involved it would appear, Mr. Chairman, that the proposed cost should be very low and we therefore ought not to accept the views of those who try to promote the idea that this is cheap insurance.
The hon. member for Vancouver South also heard Mr. MacGregor say in the course of his very impressive evidence that schemes of group insurance in Canada today run down in cost to 50 cents, 45 cents, and 42 cents per thousand per month. There are schemes of group insurance in existence in Canada today that are cheaper than this scheme. The cost of this scheme is not just 40 cents per thousand per month. The government is contributing the equivalent of eight cents per thousand per month. Mr. MacGregor stated that you could reckon the cost of this scheme at 48 cents per thousand per month, and there are in existence in Canada today group insurance schemes with smaller numbers involved than the 230,000 involved here on which the cost is less than 48 cents per thousand per month, as is provided in this bill.
Mr. MacGregor's evidence has torn to shreds and tatters this airy talk from the government about this being such a cheap scheme of group insurance. Has anyone else been asked to submit figures on cost so that we might at least test whether this is the lowest cost available? The answer, Mr. Chairman, is no. The life insurance companies offered their services but they were not asked even to quote any rates or make any studies. It was the government's decision that no one should be consulted as to any other rates, and consequently we have one rate put before us and no basis of comparison

on the part of anyone else who might have been willing to quote it. We know, according to the evidence, that this scheme carries a higher rate than is in existence in certain other schemes of group insurance in Canada today.
Now, Mr. Chairman, let us recognize also that group insurance of the kind in existence in Canada today in many group schemes is quite unlike this scheme in that this one offers no benefit except the death benefit. There are many advantages which the normal system of group insurance has which are not offered by this scheme. Surely, Mr. Chairman, that ought to be taken into account in weighing whether this is a cheap, reasonable, or expensive scheme. If hon. members look at page 1738 of the evidence they will find that Mr. MacGregor gives a catalogue of the various benefits normally written into policies of group insurance and he indicates some of them which are very valuable.
He refers to the fact that there is often an opportunity given for increasing the total amount of death benefit, and that there is provision for converting to other types of life insurance when the individual ceases to be a member of the group for any reason. He points out, in addition, that these policies of group insurance very often include disability benefits and also-and this is very important-that in these insurance schemes involving a group of employees the employer normally pays a much larger relative proportion of the total cost than the one-sixth which the government is proposing to pay under this scheme.
The government, Mr. Chairman, has of course the advantage here with respect to this type of insurance because, as we weie told by Mr. Taylor and Mr. MacGregor, the government has all the superannuation records available today, and adding the insurance to the superannuation figures on the card or record of any employee means that there does not have to be the same duplication of work as would be required if the insurance were placed elsewhere. speechtext:
It does not matter what was the overwhelming weight of evidence given before the committee. It is enough that the minister who introduced this bill thinks that it is an excellent bill. Therefore no good purpose would be served by further deliberation, further study or further consultation on the part of those upon whom exactions are to be imposed under this bill.
No, Mr. Chairman, in the government's thinking there is no place for consultation. The minister thinks this is an excellent bill and that is enough; and apparently, as far as the House of Commons is concerned, that

is to be enough for the majority in the house that normally supports the government, because this bill is to be jammed through today without those hon. members being given an opportunity even to read the evidence that was taken before the banking and commerce committee.
There are 104 pages of that evidence. Every word of it ought to be read, weighed, carefully considered and digested by every member of this house before he commits himself on a bill involving serious compulsory features. Nobody in the House of Commons or outside of it knows where the preponderant feeling of those to be affected by this bill lies with respect to it. There is not any member of this house who has any right to say that he thinks it is desired by a majority of those to be affected, either in the civil service or in the armed forces, because nobody has that kind of information. On the contrary such limited information as is available with respect to the feeling within the civil service indicates that there is a strong feeling against it and that they want time to consider it.
Mr. Chairman, if this were an optional measure, there would then be a perfect reason for the government to say, "We are not forcing this on anybody; nobody who does not desire it is required to take it". There would then be a perfectly good reason for going ahead, if it were the best scheme available, after due consideration of the possibility of improving it without its being a compulsory scheme. But when you are making it a compulsory scheme surely the minimum obligation is to know the feeling on the part of those to be affected by it.
That leads me, Mr. Chairman, to make some observations on this matter of consultation. There was a curious confusion of principle on the part of the hon. member for Ottawa West in what he had to say on the subject of consultation. I know this was not intended on his part, but I think I must make the matter quite clear. What was proposed in this matter of consultation was not that the bill be submitted to some group outside of parliament for veto. It is rather that the scheme involved in the bill should be the matter of consultation between the government on the one hand and those who are to be directly affected by the scheme on the other. It was a scheme, not a bill, that was discussed by the government, principally through the deputy minister of finance with the national joint council. But let it be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that every member on that national joint council had his lips sealed by the government.

This matter was first mooted last November. Consultations with the national joint council were held, but the members of that national joint council were told at every stage that they were not to discuss this matter with anyone outside the national joint council. Not one of them was permitted to discuss this scheme even with the executive of his own organization. There was on the part of the government an attempt to place on a group, a score of individuals, the responsibility of attempting to speak for civil servants numbering over
110.000	persons. If you look at the evidence you will see that those who sat on that national joint council, whose lips were sealed by the government, and who were denied any opportunity of consultation with those they represented, whether at the executive level or at any other level, said that they were not prepared to take that responsibility. They rebelled at the idea of having imposed upon them by the government the responsibility for speaking on this matter for over
110.000	civil servants.
I ask hon. members of this committee to weigh that fact carefully. As the hon. member for Ottawa West has said, it is true that these members sat on that national joint council as representatives of important groups of civil servants. But let us consider their position. They sat as individuals with sealed lips. Then the chairman of the banking and commerce committee-and this was a curious development-produced some newspaper reports, one I think in February and one in April, indicating that there had apparently been a leak and that the details of the scheme had leaked out. The chairman of the committee asked these five representatives of important associations of civil servants if, in the light of the fact that the cat had escaped out of the bag through these newspaper reports, they did not think there had been a satisfactory substitute for consultation. The answer given by those representatives was clear and convincing. They said that the fact that in one newspaper report details of surprising accuracy leaked out sealed their lips more tightly than ever. How could they make any comment upon a newspaper report under those circumstances? How could it be a matter of discussion by them with those they represented? They made it abundantly clear that both before and after those two newspaper reports leaked out their lips were sealed and there was no consultation.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, all of those associations of civil servants, speaking through their representatives, appeared before the committee and said that to the extent to which they had had, in one week, and one week 83276-3751
Public Service Superannuation Act only, since the bill was introduced in the house, limited and scant opportunity to consult executives or to send wires to local branches with only the most meagre details of the scheme, they asked for delay; the request was unanimous. Every one of them said that this matter ought to have further study. Every one of them said that they had not had the opportunity they ought to have had to discuss the matter with their executive and their branches. They also uniformly said that to the extent to which the opinion of their members in various places in Canada has been expressed to them in the short few days that had been available to them-just one week-strong opposition had been registered to the compulsory feature of the bill.
I think it is fair to say, Mr. Chairman, that the idea of optional insurance appealed to them. They liked the idea in general, but not on the compulsory basis. Therefore they made a plea-and it was an urgent plea in every case; an extremely strong plea-that this matter should not be hustled through now but that they should be given the opportunity of consultation.
There is no derogation from the sovereign rights of parliament, Mr. Chairman, in a matter of this kind when those who are principally affected by the measure, those whose salaries and pay cheques are hereafter to suffer deductions willy-nilly whether or not they want the insurance, come before a parliamentary committee and, with reference to a measure that has been introduced in the House of Commons and sent to that parliamentary committee for study, ask that the measure be delayed and that they be given the opportunity that I conceive to be the right of any employee of any employer to sit down with his employer and talk to his employer before that employer begins to make deductions from his pay envelope. There is the simple gist of the situation. There is no derogation from the rights of parliament involved or suggested in the kind of consultation that is sought.
Surely the federal government of this country ought, in so far as it is an employer, to try to be an exemplary employer.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, with the acquiescence in that position of the Minister of Finance, when a scheme is brought forward that does involve a compulsory imposition on every employee the employees, through their responsible organizations, have a right to be heard by the employer, to put their case before the employer and to have that case carefully

Public Service Superannuation Act considered, not brushed off in a way that is denying today to 80 per cent of the members of this house any opportunity of so much as reading this evidence, let alone weighing it and giving to it that consideration that these employees of the federal government have the right to expect. If this measure has all the merits that the government claims for it, then why should the government doubt that these merits will become apparent to the civil service when the civil service has an opportunity to study the measure? Why should the government deny to the civil service the opportunity of studying the measure and making their views upon it known?
Then there is the matter of the armed forces. That was an afterthought after the original scheme began to take shape. There was some limited consultation there, very limited indeed, but at any rate it was a form of consultation that was denied in any respect and in any degree to the civilian employees of the government. A directive was sent out by the Department of National Defence concerning the measure and a yes or no answer was sought, an expression on the part of what was thought to be "a good cross-section". We know the extent of the consultation in the case of two of the military commands. Twenty per cent was the total of the forces under the western command whose opinion was sought. The only other command concerning which we know the percentage of those consulted was the Quebec command where we were told it was about 50 per cent. That is what we know about consultation with the army. The only question put to them was: Yes or no, are you or are you not in favour of this scheme?
They were given no opportunity to express themselves on the compulsory feature. Here is what Mr. Armstrong, the assistant deputy minister of national defence, had to say on that matter as found at page 1732 of the evidence:
Q. And the directive called for a sample of opinion?
A. The directive called for a good cross-section of opinion.
Q. It was left to the area commander in each case to determine what is a good cross-section?
A. Yes.
Q. You did not stipulate?
A. No, we did not stipulate how much.
Q. I think we can appreciate the limitations of a "yes" or "no" answer. You would not expect anyone to draw an inference, Mr. Armstrong, as to what could be drawn, by way of inference, from these results as to the feeling of those consulted, if they had been given the opportunity of choosing between a compulsory plan and a plan that was not compulsory.
A. It would be quite a different question.
Q. Quite.
A. We did not ask them that.

Q. And I think you will agree no one could draw any inference as to the feeling of the men as between two such schemes as to what was done here?
A. No, I would agree that you cannot draw that inference.
That is not consultation, Mr. Chairman. We do not know how the matter was put to the limited number of men in these commands before whom it was put. We have some information about percentages in certain cases from commands in the air force and some in the navy. The lowest percentage of those in favour was in the navy in the ranks below chief petty officer. But, Mr. Chairman, we do not know how this was put before the armed forces even to the limited extent to which they were consulted. Was it done orally on parade? Was anything put before them that would enable the men being asked for a yes or no answer in a case like that really to weigh the details of a scheme of this kind?
Now, sir, in conclusion I ask this question with reference to delay. All that is asked for by those who represent these valued civil servants of Canada is delay, an opportunity to consult with those whom they represent, an opportunity to study the measure and an opportunity then to put their views before the government. The existing insurance scheme is still in effect. Under it 13,000 policies are in effect and, as Mr. MacGregor says, the scheme is working quite satisfactorily. This is a measure of very high importance. It has been talked about for a long time. There is no desperate urgency about it. As long as the existing insurance scheme stands those who appeared before us indicated that they did want to have the opportunity of consultation, that they did not want to see this measure rushed through now.
We realize that if this had been brought in at an earlier stage of the session by the government, as a measure of this kind ought to have been, there could have been an opportunity for consultation. But here we are within a matter of a few days apparently before the end of the session and we are asked to deny to these representatives of the civil servants the opportunity they ask for consultation. Mr. Chairman, if this matter stands for that adequate opportunity the measure is not killed. It is not killed unless the government decides to kill it because the government can introduce this measure or, I would hope, a measure without the compulsory feature in it, at the next session after there has been an adequate opportunity for consultation. That is what we are asking.
Indeed, sir, the civil servants, those who are to be affected by it, are not even being given the opportunity to "take it or leave it".

The government does not even say to them as individuals: "Take it or leave it". The government is rather holding a club over their heads today and saying: Well, you had better take this holus-bolus, the whole thing, or we will withdraw the measure and we will not introduce it again. What an attitude for the government to take! What irresponsibility! Delay does not involve the death of a measure of this kind unless the government itself chooses to impose the death sentence on the measure.
I plead again with the government not to press this measure, not to deny the opportunity for consultation to those who are going to be affected by it. I plead with the government to put aside just for once the attitude that they show so often, this attitude that I can best sum up in these words: "We will show you who is boss around here." We have seen that in this house. Let the government not take that attitude toward the civil servants. We in the opposition grow accustomed to it, but on this occasion when the civil service is involved can the government not relax just a little bit? Cannot the government give a little time? Cannot the government be reasonable about this measure, and sit down and discuss it in an amicable way as between employer and employee, both representing responsibilities that they have to carry and yet both realizing that they have an important responsibility to each other and that this measure should, so far as is humanly possible, be the best measure that the combined wisdom of the government on the one hand and those who are going to be affected by it on the other hand can devise?
Even in the limited time available, these representative civils servants' associations have brought forward a large number of changes that they desire. Perhaps some of them could be incorporated with time, and some of them perhaps cannot. I do not know. But I do know that they are all entitled to serious consideration because they are put forward by people carrying some responsibility in this matter. They are simply asking for delay. What right have we to shut the door in their faces, and deny them that delay for the purpose of consultation?

Mr. Chairman, as a member of the banking and commerce committee I, too, was somewhat disturbed to find that there was a considerable measure of opposition to this bill coming from the civil service. As a matter of fact I was undecided
14, 1954
Public Service Superannuation Act in my own mind as to just what was the right line to take with regard to this legislation, in view of that particular opposition. I took the advice of the hon. member for Eglinton before he gave it, and read the evidence given before the committee. I propose to read some of that evidence before I have finished this afternoon. I do this because there were some things that were not read this morning which strike me as being quite relevant to the matter.
I do think the government is due for quite severe criticism for the method in which this legislation was introduced. I am quite prepared to go along with the hon. member for Eglinton and others who have protested against the government's failure to consult the civil service, and also against the late date at which the measure was introduced in the house. I also think the minister himself perhaps is due for some criticism for the rather disingenuous way in which he introduced the legislation-that is to say, his determined effort to present it, not as a group insurance measure but as some other kind of measure. I can understand why he tried to do that; I can understand his reasons for doing it. Nevertheless I think it helped to add confusion to the picture.
The hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Peace River have based most of their objections to the legislation on its compulsory nature. I suppose from one point of view one might say that we have no right to force things down people's throats, no matter how good for them, if they do not want them. On the other hand, today we are demanding of our government a degree of responsibility for public servants that is perhaps quite new in our history. I think most of us will agree that we expect the government to treat public servants with justice, and perhaps with a fair measure of generosity. I suspect that the families of many civil servants have been treated with considerable generosity on an ad hoc basis. For that reason I think we are justified in suggesting that if we are going to accept the principle that as a community we are responsible for those who serve us, then we have the right to demand that they comply with the most efficient and economical method of discharging that responsibility toward them. So I think we can discount that particular aspect of the opposition to the bill.
It has been said-indeed it was so indicated by civil servants who spoke before the banking and commerce committee-that there are a number of civil servants who object to this measure. At first glance I can readily see that there would be quite a number who

Public Service Superannuation Act would have objection to it. Those who have no dependents, and do not expect to see their lives take such a turn that they will have dependents during their service in the public service, would naturally view this legislation with a certain amount ol misgiving. 1 refer of course to that large body of female civil servants many of whom, I presume-the younger ones-approach this matter as they do in so many other occupations, with the idea in mind that before long they are going to enter holy bonds and will no longer require the sort of coverage this legislation proffers to them. I think that is an understandable point of view on their part.
On the other hand we can counter that, I believe, by pointing out that very likely these young ladies will marry young men who are themselves in the public service, and the contributions they make to the scheme before marriage will have a direct bearing upon their own future, at some future date, should their husbands die. In fact, I think that if we examine most cases we will find that most people, no matter what their circumstances may be, have some relatives or semi-dependents who will be adversely affected both financially and otherwise by the death of that person. They might not always be conscious of it. Perhaps many young people do not realize that when a human being dies it is somebody's business to dispose of that human being. That in itself is quite a responsibility that falls on somebody else's shoulders.
We may not always be conscious of the fact-certainly a single person might not- that at some point such a person would present a problem to somebody else. This is a method of dealing with that problem. It has been suggested that one of the objectionable features in the legislation is that the contributors may contribute all their lives, right up to the time of retirement, and not receive a penny in return. That is quite true. But I believe that objection results from drawing a false analogy between this type of insurance and ordinary endowment life insurance. I believe a much more accurate analogy can be drawn between this sort of legislation and fire or accident insurance. And I am sure no one would suggest it is outrageous for us to have to pay fire insurance premiums on our houses and never have any fires. Because that, after all, is the basis of the objection to this legislation. The purpose of the measure is to protect relatives from the disastrous results of untimely death in the public service. And for that reason I do not think we can expect to have any

This morning the hon. member quoted from the proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce, and suggested there was evidence to show that the scheme was much more expensive than need be, or than could be provided by private insurance companies. I do not read the evidence in that way, at all. In fact, I find quite different evidence given here. Yes, I have the reference here. It is to be found at page 1740. In answer to a question Mr. MacGregor had this to say:
Q. You mentioned before the supper hour, some companies, such as the aircraft companies, and chain store companies, had a low net premium which would compare with this 40 cents. Might not that be for younger employees?
A. In every case, doctor, there is an explanation. I could cite groups where the cost is relatively high as well as the ones which I have cited where costs are relatively low. In the last instance the explanation is usually that the average age is very low or that the maximum amount is very low for the higher ages.
On page 1747 Mr. MacGregor gave further evidence which I thought was very interesting. This was with regard to the necessity for keeping the premium low in this scheme, because young single men, according to Mr. MacGregor, could go to a company and get an individual one-year term policy for probably $7.50 or $7.20 a thousand per annum, which works out of course to sixty cents or a little over sixty cents per thousand. Therefore it was said in those schemes to which he was referring we had to keep it low down otherwise these young people would not participate in it. The point that occurs to me, Mr. Chairman, is that these young people eventually will become middle-aged people and finally they will become old people and will not be able to derive benefits from those schemes.

The principal objection as I see it, the factor that the hon. member for Eglinton finally got around to agreeing to this morning, was that the scheme was probably a fairly good one but that it was being forced down the throats of civil servants against their wills. He might be right in that. It is quite possible that there are a number of civil servants-in fact I know there are; I have had some of them speak to me-who make very strenuous objections to this legislation; but, on the other hand on balance we have to support it because in this day and age we do assume, as I say, a tremendous amount of responsibility for our public servants, and because we assume that responsibility we have the right to say on what terms we shall discharge that responsibility, and we demand co-operation of public servants who, after all, also demand that responsibility from us. We have the right that they should co-operate with us.
It has been suggested of course that the great shortcoming is the fact that people pay in and when they are old they draw nothing out of it. Well, I think we have to face this fact, Mr. Chairman, this very harsh and bitter fact. As an equity in a building gets lower and lower as that building gets older and older, so we have to accept the fact that when we get fairly well along we have very little but sentimental value for our relatives and that we should not expect to have a cash value at that time. This thing is designed to cover those who have a cash value for their relatives during that period when they have a cash value. When they get past that stage then those relatives presumably have reached the age where they can assume responsibility for them. Therefore while, as I say, I was disturbed by this objection on the part of the civil servants, in answering that, as I see the course I should follow, I have, after reading over the evidence and thinking over the matter very carefully, come to the conclusion we should support this measure, particularly as Mr. MacGregor in his evidence to the banking and commerce committee suggested that it will be necessary to review the rates from time to time to see that they carry out the purpose of this legislation.

speechtext:
In addition to the civil
servants who are affected by this bill there are over 112,000 servicemen, men in the armed forces. If the civil servants had an opportunity of expressing their views on this proposed legislation, the same facilities for the expression of views did not exist in respect of the men in the armed services. Word was sent out in a coded message to the commanders in the various areas and it was
Public Service Superannuation Act marked "confidential". One can easily imagine what would be the action taken by an ordinary commanding officer who received a confidential message in code. He would express his opinion as to the effect of this legislation on the men under his command. But it would appear that some security was broken because early in April I received a wire from British Columbia, the essence of which was: We understand that the men of the armed services are being told that they are not to take out any more life insurance with private companies because there is going to be a compulsory life insurance scheme introduced by the government. They did not believe that they had any choice whatever in this matter. They believed that they were taking out a life insurance scheme in which they would be able to make payments which would accumulate over the years of their service and, eventually, when they died, there would be benefits coming to their estate. But when you come to read the provisions of this bill and the purpose for which it is brought in you sense that they are not going to get any life insurance in the usual understanding of that term which would be handed down to their estate, but that they are going to pay a yearly premium against the possibility that they will die during that year.
The purpose of the bill, as it was given to the committee, is that it is to cover the cost of the last illness and death and those expenses which are consequential upon it. I should like you to consider for a minute how it is going to apply to the servicemen. I say that it will apply only during the year in which they are making their contribution. They are in fact gambling that they will die this year. There are not many young men at the ages of 18 to 21 who want to bet that they are going to die in the next twelve months. Actually the government is betting on an odds-on favourite, and they protect themselves by saying that when the serviceman reaches approximately the age that he may expect to die, namely, seventy, he will not be able to get any of the benefits at all, and all the money that he has paid in during his service and afterwards, if he desires to go on contributing, will be lost. I say there are few yoting men of service age who would want to enter into a bet of that kind.
The average man who joins the service is between the ages of 18 and 25, and the normal term of enlistment is for from three years to five years. During that time, when he comes up for his enlistment first and his enrolment, or when he takes on again, he has to be subjected to a very thorough

Public Service Superannuation Act medical examination. He knows that he is fit. The very duties that he has to perform keep him fit. His chances of dying at an early age fortunately are very remote. But this is to provide for his last illness and burial expenses. One of the conditions upon which he enters the service is that he will receive free medical attention and, in addition, if he dies during his service the burial expenses will be paid on his behalf. Therefore, as far as the main purpose of this bill is concerned, the young soldier, sailor, or airman is not going to get anything in so far as the major benefits are concerned.
If upon the completion of his service he decides that he is going back into civilian life he may continue the payments plus an additional contribution. If he retires, as most of these young men do, before he is 30 years of age he has got to keep on making contributions for 30 or 40 years until he finally reaches the age of 70 when he will not be called upon to make any more contributions because he will not receive any benefits after that.
I would like the committee to consider what this is going to mean in so far as the cost of administration on the part of the government is concerned. Figures given in "Canada's Defence Program", the so-called white paper for 1954-55, give us some idea of the turnover in the armed services. The wastage in the navy, army and air force during the year 1951-52 amounted to 11,903; during the year 1952-53 the wastage was 16,658; and during the year 1953-54 it was 16,297. I think these figures demonstrate how these accounts are going to pyramid. Is the Department of National Defence going to send out monthly notices to the various men who have retired to the effect that their 40 cents is due and they are in arrears for the preceding month?

It may be that the Minister of Finance and Minister of Veterans Affairs got together and discussed this, and it may be they have decided that the pensions now being paid to the 19,700 widows of war veterans in Canada are not adequate, and that some form for increasing their pensions should be adopted. If that is the case then the simplest thing to do would be to bring in an increased scale of pension for the war widows. I do not believe there would be very much objection in this house if that were done. But this is a very roundabout way of making provision for an increased pension for the widows of the future.
Then, again, the man who is on active service has an opportunity of taking advantage of the veterans insurance scheme. I am not going to extend my remarks beyond that otherwise than to allow my memory to wander back some time to that period when I first joined the services close to 50 years ago. At that time the recruit, more or less as a matter of course, bought the beer for his corporal. Under this scheme it would seem that the private soldier is expected to contribute towards his colonel's coffin, and I do not think that will appeal very much to the average private soldier.
However, the main feature about this matter is that I am convinced that the public relations regarding this bill have been extremely bad, and that the men in the armed services have not understood the provisions of this scheme. I therefore think the minister would really be extremely well advised, in so far as the armed services are concerned, to allow them to have a second look at the bill and have the opinions of the majority of the men who are going to make a contribution towards this scheme thoroughly canvassed.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think there is a great deal that one need add to what has already been said, except that, in addition to the reasons that have been given for opposing it, there is another one that occurs to me. It appears to me that this is what might be called paternalism run rampant. From what I have heard of it and from the summaries I have had of what took place in the banking and commerce committee it appears to me that the government has said: We think it would be desirable if everybody had an insurance policy on his life; therefore we are going to see to it that, because we think it is a good thing, everybody we can force to have one will be forced to have it whether he wants it or not. It might be a good thing if everyone in the country had an insurance policy on his life, but I am surprised to find the government which, on occasion, asserts its belief in leaving to the individual, so far as it can be done, control over his own destiny, adopting the position that we are now going to tell the people what is best for them in a matter in which previously no government has ever arrogated to itself the power to compel them to accept a benevolent ruling and is going to put the legislation through whether or not the people concerned consent to it or want it. It is truly the worst form of paternalism rim rampant.
Benevolent paternalism is all very well or good intentions are all very well in their place; but when good intentions, the benefit of which is not the subject of agreement by those affected, is going to have the sanction of legislation and of dictate behind it, I think it then becomes the duty of those who believe in the individual being given the maximum control of his destiny consistent with the position that his own actions shall


not impinge upon or interfere with the exercise of his neighbour's freedom, to say: No; you shall not, whether out of any benevolent motives or not, exercise this form of dictatorship.
On the basis of that approach to the matter it seems to me that we have not much alternative but to oppose the present bill. I think it would have put us all in a great deal better position had there been given to the civil servants affected the time and opportunity for a greater study of the matter so that we would know whether or not, in fact, a majority of them approved it. If they want it and if it were to be clearly indicated that they want it, then I suppose it would be stepping beyond the bounds of our duty to say: No, you shall not have it.
However, as I understand the position, there has not been any clear-cut request of that sort for it. The government has simply come along and decided that this would be a good thing for the civil servants themselves. In the absence of their being able to bring to us clear proof that the people concerned actually want it, it is my opinion that, as we have the situation now, in the presence of a considerable volume of evidence from them that they do not want it, we have to say to the government: No; you shall not impose your idea of what is good on the people who themselves do not agree with your ideas.
I think also that when the government takes to itself the right to dictate to the armed forces, in addition to the civil service, on matters of this kind then, for the reasons so cogently put forward by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, we should say to them: Here, you have got to confine your activities within reasonable bounds; you can lay down conditions of service in so far as hours of work and times of work are concerned but you certainly cannot say to people that if they are going to work in the civil service or join the armed forces they have to join this compulsory insurance scheme. To me, that is carrying benevolence to the point of absurdity.
