speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL HIGHWAY TRANSPORT
speechtext:
second reading of Bill No. 474, respecting extra-provincial motor vehicle transport.
He said: The house will recall that on February 23 last, following the decision of the privy council in the Winner case, I made a statement in this house with respect to interprovincial and international highway transport. I stated at that time that in our view it would not be in the public interest to have a divided jurisdiction with provincial boards controlling the traffic within the provinces and a federal board controlling the traffic moving between the provinces or between a province and the United States, and that for this amongst other reasons the government was reluctant to enter this field and thereby bring about divided jurisdiction.
I also stated that I proposed to call a conference of provincial ministers having jurisdiction over highways to discuss the problems arising herein and to endeavour to find a common ground on the best way to regulate and control highway transport, whether intraprovincial, interprovincial or international. A federal-provincial conference on the control and regulation of interprovincial and international highway transport was duly called and convened at Ottawa on April 26. The federal government and the governments of all the provinces except Newfoundland were represented at this conference. Newfoundland was not represented as the government of that province was not interested in this particular problem.
At the outset of the conference the representatives of the federal government indicated to the representatives of the provinces that the conference had been called to ascertain the views of the provinces in regard to assuming jurisdiction over interprovincial and international highway transport, and whether there was a disposition on the part of the provinces to assume such responsibility. The provincial delegates at the conference agreed on the broad proposition that it would be desirable for the provinces to assume jurisdiction over interprovincial and international highway transport, and various means of reaching this objective were discussed. Two principal methods were considered. First it was proposed by certain of the provinces that appropriate amendments be made to the British North America Act to ensure that

Motor Vehicle Transport jurisdiction over highway traffic and control is vested in the provinces. This proposal was not considered to be practicable at this time and was not acceptable to the federal government.
The second proposal placed before the conference was that legislation be enacted by the federal parliament to provide for the control and regulation of the transportation of passengers and goods by motor vehicle between a province and a point outside the province with the control to be exercised by a provincial authority in like manner as control is exercised under provincial law. Such a system of provincial control over extra-provincial transport would leave the situation in much the same condition as before the decision of the courts in the Winner case. A draft bill was submitted to the conference and certain revisions were made.
The bill which is now before the house is the result of the work of the conference and has been approved in principle by all of the provinces that were represented except the province of Quebec. The bill provides that each province will have control over that portion of the transport undertaking that is carried on in that province. The bill accordingly requires an extra-provincial transport undertaking operating into or through a province to hold an operating licence if provincial law requires an operating licence for a local undertaking. The provincial board is authorized to grant this licence, which is in the nature of a franchise, and in so doing the provincial board follows the rules applicable to local undertakings. In other words, the provincial board is authorized to license extra-provincial transport undertakings in the same manner as it licenses local undertakings. This method of conferring power on provincial boards to license extra-provincial undertakings is considered by the law officers of the crown to be within the competence of parliament.
The bill also makes provision for regulation of tariffs and tolls charged by federal carriers for the transport of goods and passengers. The same pattern is followed as in the case of the operating licence. If tariffs and tolls for local traffic are regulated by provincial law, then the tariffs and tolls for extraprovincial traffic are to be determined and regulated by the provincial board in the same way as tariffs and tolls are determined and regulated for local traffic.
In order to deal with unforeseen circumstances which may possibly arise in the future in connection with highway transport movements for natiqnal defence and also in respect
TMr. Chevrier.]
of international agreements and other extraordinary cases, it has been considered advisable to provide for exemption by the governor in council of the whole or any part of an extra-provincial undertaking from all or any of the provisions of the act. This is in the nature of a safety provision which will not be used unless there are cases of real difficulty in the operation of the act.
As this bill is one which concerns the provinces individually as well as collectively, and as it is not desired to transfer the responsibility for the regulation of extra-provincial transport to any province that is unwilling to accept this charge, the bill provides that the act shall come into force in any province only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council.
Penalties are provided to ensure compliance with the act.
The bill is a short one and is readily understood. It is the government's answer to the difficult problem of how the provinces can be enabled to control and regulate highway transport crossing their boundaries and using their highways. The control of road traffic using provincial highways is essentially a matter for the provincial boards which are established and well qualified for this purpose. The solution proposed by this bill appears to be a satisfactory one within the framework of our constitution and I trust will commend itself to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR REGULATION OF INTERPROVINCIAL AND INTERNATIONAL HIGHWAY TRANSPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us is one that comes to the house at a stage in the session when there might be some suggestion that there would be difficulty in obtaining the information that ordinarily would be obtained without any question in connection with legislation of this kind. I am sure that if the legislation came before the house early in the session, immediately there would be a statement by the government that it was going to be referred to an appropriate committee which would hear evidence and, through the hearing of evidence, hon. members would be informed as to the effect of legislation of this kind in dealing with the extremely involved and difficult problem presented.
The statement made by the minister is a brief one and deals with what has taken place recently. The subject matter, however, is one that has been before the House of Commons, the parliament of Canada and the people of this country generally for some considerable time. As hon. members of the house are well aware, this problem is one which was the subject matter of consideration by a royal commission appointed by the

government. Members of the House of Commons are also aware of the fact that this matter was dealt with earlier by the Supreme Court of Canada, at the instance of the government of Canada. There was, in fact, a judgment of the supreme court rendered on October 22, 1951. That judgment, given almost three years ago, had the effect of declaring, with only minor limitations, that this was a subject which came fully under the authority of the federal government, through the provisions of section 92 (10) of the British North America Act. The applicable part of that section is as follows:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:-
(a) Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province;
In the interpretation of that section it has been found that this means of transportation, as an extra-provincial means of transportation, came substantially under the authority of the government of Canada. Not satisfied with such limitations as were contained in the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, the provinces carried the appeal to the privy council. By judgment of February 22, 1954, as has been mentioned by the minister, it was declared that authority over extraprovincial or interprovincial transportation of this kind came under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada.
I would point out that substantially the position in which the matter is now before us was declared in October of 1951, and that this is not something that has suddenly come upon the government. It is something that has been under consideration for a considerable time. It is something that could have been discussed in conference with the provinces on earlier occasions. It is something that could have been discussed immediately after the judgment of the privy council.
We now have this bill before us on the 14th day of June, for second reading. It deals with highway transportation, which today is an extremely important part of the general system of transportation in Canada. Surely, when this subject is to be dealt with it would be appropriate that it be referred to a committee where representatives of those organizations engaging in transportation activities of this and other types would have an opportunity to present their arguments and hon. members thereby benefit from the information which would be placed before them.
The minister said that the conference sought to find common ground. Actually there is little evidence of common ground
Motor Vehicle Transport other than the fact that responsibility over extra-provincial and interprovincial highway transportation, as well as transportation within the provinces, is to be under the authority of boards set up in the provinces themselves. There certainly is no evidence of common ground as to procedure. There certainly is no evidence of common ground as to a method of supervising interprovincial or extra-provincial transportation; there certainly is no evidence of common ground as to rates or otherwise. We have before us a bill which produces an interesting result.
The government of Canada has been engaged now for several years in seeking to establish the position that it has full responsibility over extra-provincial and interprovincial transportation. Now that has been declared to be the law by the privy council. As soon as that is declared law, the government of Canada proposes to hand over to the provinces the responsibility for which the provinces have been fighting in the course of several years. It certainly seems a strange thing that large sums of public money would be spent to establish this position, and then once the position is established the authority for licensing and generally supervising this type of transportation should be placed right in the hands of boards appointed by the provinces under the provincial governments. That may be the best solution. That may be the solution which will work out most satisfactorily. I submit, Mr. Speaker, nothing has been placed before us to indicate why this is being done after all the legal activity which has been devoted to this subject for so many years, and after the inquiry which was conducted under the authority of this government when a royal commission investigated this extremely important subject.
The trucking services are giving very valuable services to our enterprises of so many kinds. Our railways are giving invaluable service; so are other means of transportation. Surely, in attempting to deal with this problem, we should have information before us such as we have obtained in similar cases, and the procedure should be followed which has been found to be satisfactory in those cases.
I recognize, as I am sure every hon. member does, that there are special problems in connection with highway transportation. There is first of all the fact that every province has responsibility for the construction of the highways within the province, and that the provincial authorities must of necessity gauge the relationship of that transportation to the capacity of those highways to carry services of those kinds. There is also the fact that we must recognize the vital part that this transportation plays now in the

Motor Vehicle Transport whole economy of Canada. What is done should recognize its place in our economy. That demands inquiry; that demands information. It demands an appropriate opportunity to question those who are experts in this field and to form judgments based on information of that kind.
I would point out there is another aspect to this problem. We are dealing not only with highway transportation made available by vehicles owned by Canadian companies and individuals; we are also considering transportation provided by vehicles owned by companies and individuals in the United States. It is of interest to find that as recently as June 7 this dispatch was carried from Washington by the United Press:
In a move admittedly aimed at Canadian truckers, the House of Representatives voted today to subject operators of foreign trucks using American highways to interstate commerce commission safety regulations.
The report then went on to deal with this question and to indicate that certain provisions were to apply to the truckers using the highways of the United States which had come there from Canada. Surely, this suggests to us the desirability of information from those with direct knowledge of this type of activity which will inform us as to what should be done here to deal with a similar situation within our own country.
I would point out further that there is one clause of this bill which produces a very striking result, namely clause 5, which reads as follows:
The governor in council may exempt any person or the whole or any part of an extra-provincial undertaking or any extra-provincial transport from all or any of the provisions of this act.
I understood from what the minister said that the bill was so designed that the government would be able to take appropriate steps to assure certain things being done. As I read this clause it is simply one which authorizes the governor in council, or in other words the government, to exempt any person or the whole or any part of an extra-provincial undertaking or any extra-provincial transport from any or all of the provisions of this legislation.
That, Mr. Speaker, is hardly something that provides for positive action. It is something which merely provides for negative action which would remove whatever advantages the government now submits can be obtained from the operation of this legislation. I think we should have a clearer explanation of the full import of clause 5, before we are called upon to deal with this bill. The truth is that under clause 5 the whole of this bill can be swept aside by order in council at any time. If it is important that this bill be


now put into effect, it is equally important that this legislation remain in effect until parliament has been consulted in regard to the matter, unless there are some reasons which have not been placed before us for the extremely wide power which would be conferred upon the government by the adopting of the measure as it stands.
This is an important subject, Mr. Speaker. This is a subject which is of interest to Canadians generally. In this tremendous country of ours, with its expanding development, transportation by rail, by highway, air or water is all part and parcel of that dramatic development which is now taking place.
Surely it is appropriate that we should assure the most effective type of legislation we can have when we are called upon to deal with any aspect of this great problem of transportation. If it was sufficiently important to appoint a royal commission to inquire into this subject, if it was sufficiently important to carry this argument through to the privy council, then it is sufficiently important that the subject matter of this bill be now referred to a standing committee of the house.
It is my intention to move that this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to a standing committee of the house. The committee to which I propose it should be referred is the committee on banking and commerce, because this is essentially a question of commerce within Canada and between Canada and the United States. I therefore believe it is appropriate that the committee on banking and commerce should deal with this as quickly as possible.
There is plenty of time to refer this immediately and call before that committee those who can speak with knowledge and experience in regard to the various aspects of this subject, and give us the information we should have before we pass a bill of this kind. In making this proposal I am certainly not reflecting on the judgment of those who represented the provinces in the conference which took place here. It would indeed be a very surprising thing if the representatives of the provinces did not welcome a bill which gave to them the full powers which they asserted before the courts should be theirs in any event. It would, in fact, be most unnatural if they should carry a legal battle into the courts and assert that they have this right of licensing and then, when the act is placed before them which confers that right by legislation passed by the parliament of Canada, that they should suggest they would not welcome it.

That is all that has happened in the bill now before us, except for the very sweeping and, in fact, complete reservation of power contained in clause 5 for reasons which have not yet been fully explained to us.
Having said that, may I also say I recognize that because of the delay in dealing with this subject a situation now exists which calls for attention. The fact is that because of the judgment of the privy council it is perfectly apparent that there is need of some kind of legislation which will make it possible to deal with some of the very irregular things that are happening at this time.
Whatever may be said of this legislation, the government must accept full responsibility for the legislation placed before us. If it is unsatisfactory, if it is limited in its effect, if it fails to carry out some of the purposes which the government on other occasions has stated it had in mind, then the responsibility for that must rest entirely with the government.
The government must also accept full responsibility for the delay. We could have had this simple measure before us weeks ago; we could have had this simple measure before us perhaps years ago if, after the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, consultations had taken place with the provinces such as have recently taken place. If, in fact, it was intended only to carry out a procedure of this kind which gives to the provinces the very kind of supervision for which they were fighting in the courts, then that could have been done at any time within the past few years.

In the first place, while it is true that the Supreme Court of Canada handed down its decision in the Winner case in 1951, there was an appeal from that decision to the privy council. If the federal government had attempted to obtain the views of the provinces while the judgment was under appeal, I do not think the provinces would have welcomed a conference. I do not think they would have listened to the federal government; and, in

And what confirms that last opinion is this, that the judgment of the privy council in fact varied that of the Supreme Court of Canada. Then my hon. friend says that there were weeks of delay in bringing the matter before the house. Let us see what happened. Well, now, we have determined against that after very careful consideration, and we have invited the provinces, who are the ones responsible for this kind of traffic, to come here and discuss this matter, and we have asked them whether or not they felt like taking this over. They said, or at least one did, "Well, we would prefer to do it by amendment to the constitution". We said, "Well, we have no authority to deal with that, and in any event that is not practicable at the present time". They said, "Well, if it is not, then we shall go along with you in this kind of legislation". We sat down and we drafted, after quite a considerable length of time, a bill the principle of which is contained in this bill. In fact it is practically the same bill with a very small change.
What would be the effect of referring this to a committee?
What is the principle?

The effect of referring this to a committee would be to hear representations from those who are opposed to the manner in which we are doing this. If anyone has looked at the history of extra-provincial transport in this house since 1935 we will find that we will be here not for one week, two weeks or three weeks, we will be here for months discussing this very matter and hearing representations about the manner in which and the means whereby this should be done.
Why did we proceed to act in the way in which we have? For several reasons. We felt that we did not have the necessary experience nor the necessary staff or personnel to deal with this kind of traffic. After all, the provinces have been dealing with this traffic for years; it is their business; and all they will be doing by means of this enabling legislation will be to extend the powers which they possess under provincial legislation to cover extra-provincial undertakings. Then, we have not the staff; we have not a board. And what board would we establish, the board of transport commissioners? That is the logical board. Do you know what would happen if we were ever to do that? There would be a series of representations by the truckers, by the shippers, against the board. They would say: "That is a railway board; it is not a trucking board. Give us a trucking board. You are not fair to us". Anyone in this house knows that this is a very complex matter, and therefore, if we wanted to be fair to the trucking industry, which is a big industry, taking on more and more importance in Canada because of the development of highways, we would probably be doing them an injustice if we were

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Bill No. 474, clause 1; shall the clause carry?

At the time of the adjournment at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I was discussing the principle of the bill which is contained in clause 1. In view of the discussions in the previous hours and the statements made by the minister and the Minister of Justice, I have taken the opportunity to make a further study of this bill. In view of that study I should like to continue my remarks on the principle of it and perhaps, in my statements, to ask certain questions which I think are of importance.
I can say that in principle I agree with the intent of the minister on the introduction of this bill, namely to give to the provinces of Canada the power of control over extraprovincial motor vehicles. However, on reading the bill I have in my mind certain doubts which I should like to have clarified at this time, and I think perhaps there are doubts in the minds of others. As I understand the situation, the courts of the land have declared that the constitutional and jurisdictional control of extra-provincial motor vehicle transport is within the federal powers. In view of that decision-and I think it is accepted by all-the government has introduced an act authorizing the provinces to exercise a power of jurisdiction which under the constitution is declared to be strictly a federal power. My first question therefore is this: Will the Minister of Justice clarify the situation with regard to the jurisdictional power, when the highest courts have declared that the constitutional jurisdictional power is federal?
As I understand constitutional law, there are three ways in which the difficulty can be overcome. One is by an amendment to the British North America Act. The second is by the passage of an act requiring ancillary legislation by a province. The third is by the passage of an act which is of a permissive nature. In view of the fact that the constitutional jurisdiction in this matter has been declared by the courts to be strictly federal, I am going to presume that this legislation is of a permissive nature because

of a section of the act which says that it will come into force in a province only upon the issue of a proclamation of the governor in council declaring it to be in force in that province. I presume that it is by proclamation of an act of a permissive nature that the government is introducing an act giving power to the provinces, although the courts have declared that it is strictly a federal responsibility. I think that is the first question that should be clarified at this time.
Going on from that point, because I am certain that the Minister of Justice has taken note of it, I follow on to the general principle of the bill. As I have said before, I think the government has reached a right conclusion in believing that this should be a matter of provincial jurisdiction. But in principle, I cannot find where the government, under this act, is giving to the provinces extra-provincial powers with respect to motor vehicle transport. I have read carefully all the sections of the bill and I cannot find in any of them any power which is not now exercised by the provinces of Canada. In view of the recent court decision, perhaps they may have been operating illegally. Perhaps that is so. I do not know. But in the various sections of Bill No. 474 I cannot see where, in the matter of interprovincial responsibility, they are being given	one	more	power	than theyhave exercised	for	years	with	regard	tolicensing, tariffs	and	tolls.This is supposed to be an extra-provincial motor vehicle transport bill. There too I cannot find a section of this bill whereby there is any authority or set-up between the provinces by means of which we can get around all the' problems of the past in connection with extra-provincial transportation. Under this act the powers of the provinces are clear with respect to licensing, tolls and so forth. But	when the	trucker hits	the
border between British Columbia and Alberta, as I read the bill he then comes under the complete control or authority of Alberta; and the same situation prevails with respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan and with respect to Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Where is this new set-up-which to put the matter quite bluntly, I have been hoping for-of co-operation, collaboration, understanding and agreement between the provinces? I cannot find it in this bill. Perhaps I have missed it. If so, I know the minister will set me right. I know that I am not alone in missing it; a great many of us in this chamber have missed that set-up.
There is something else in the principle of this bill which I think is of the utmost 83276-377
Motor Vehicle Transport importance. I understand that at the recent conference the provinces did not all agree on this matter. If I am incorrect in my statement, I hope the minister will straighten me out immediately. I understand that the province on the Pacific coast and the provinces on the Atlantic coast agreed. One other province did not.
What is the position with respect to extraprovincial transport if you cannot get from a province in the middle of Canada to those on the east or west or vice versa because one province has not agreed to Bill No. 474? Does that mean that the province that has not entered into the agreement, or perhaps a province that might withdraw later, can cause a Balkan blockade of truck transport east and west from the Pacific to the Atlantic? I ask that question because of the principle involved. I cannot see anything in the bill whereby the federal government, in handing over this jurisdiction to the provinces, takes any authority itself with respect to licensing in order to protect the provinces that come into the agreement and provide for free access across Canada even if one province does not enter the agreement.
In other words, any one province can block the intent of the government and the minister to establish a free system of extraprovincial motor transport across Canada. I cannot see anything in the bill which gives the federal government any power whatsoever if any one province wants to block the other provinces of Canada so far as motor vehicle transport is concerned. That is a very important matter to me and I hope the minister will discuss it. As I said, first of all where does the power arise under this bill, which is of a permissive nature? In the second place, where is the extraprovincial arrangement? For, as I read the legislation, every province has always exercised every power contained in the bill? Where is the set-up to bring about correlation and co-operation so far as the arrangements are concerned? You are granting to the provinces what has been declared by law to be a federal power. I agree with that, but where does the legislation contain any power whereby the federal government will be able to see to it that no one province can interfere with the application, implementation and meaning of the legislation, the purpose of which is to ensure freer access across Canada and to avoid any stalemates so far as vehicular transport is concerned?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to deal with the questions which my hon. friend has raised, and if in the course of my

Motor Vehicle Transport remarks I do not cover all the points or there are still some legal difficulties I will ask my colleague, the Minister of Justice, to deal more fully with the legal points that are raised. My hon. friend seeks to inquire how, if by virtue of the judgment qf the courts the power to deal with this matter lies with the federal government, as it does, it is possible to give the provinces control such as we seek to do in this bill. He suggested that after studying the matter there were three methods by which it could be done. Perhaps I might say to him that there are two methods by which one could proceed.
First there is the method of enacting federal legislation and taking advantage of the powers that were determined to belong to the federal government under the British North America Act. We have decided against that. There is more than one method by which we might authorize the provinces to exercise this jurisdiction. It could be done by legislation by reference. That, I understand, is of doubtful legal validity. It could be done by delegation, and it could be done in this manner. The courts have held that this is a perfectly legal way in which to do it, namely, to give to provincial boards, not to provincial legislatures but to provincial boards, the same authority to deal with extra-provincial traffic as they have to deal with provincial traffic. Parliament has already conferred such authority on provincial boards as in the case of the Prince Edward Island potato marketing board and a number of others with which I need not deal.
That is a legal matter which was gone into carefully at the conference. Most of the attorneys general were present and all of us agreed that if it were to be done this was the best method by which to do it. Therefore I am accepting their view on it, and I do not think there is any doubt about the legality of this procedure.
The hon. member also stated that he could not find any place in this legislation where the government is giving the provinces any jurisdiction over extra-provincial transportation. That is contained in sections 3 and 4. I do not know whether I will be out of order in dealing with them at this time, but the powers the federal government has to control extra-provincial undertakings it gives to these provincial boards in the same way as these provincial boards control provincial undertakings. Again, it certainly was the view of the attorneys general who were present at the conference that this was the most practical way in which to do it.
May I ask a question? Can the minister tell me how what is provided for in section 3, to which he has referred, is any different from what goes on now?

I am not suggesting it is any different from what goes on now. Coupled with what I said in my earlier remarks on second reading of the bill, the effect of the statement I make now is that we want the provinces to continue to regulate and control extra-provincial transport undertakings in the same way as they are controlling provincial transportation at this time.
Can we agree on that?

My hon. friend then says: What will happen when traffic moving out of British Columbia arrives at the border of Alberta? What will happen when traffic moving out of another province arrives at the border of the province which has not agreed to this arrangement? The answer is quite clear. The law will be exactly the same as it is now. As I stated earlier, there is one province that did not see fit to give its concurrence to this legislation. The province of Quebec in its wisdom submitted at the conference that it would prefer a constitutional amendment. I doubt if the constitutional amendment requested by that province was the same amendment in substance as that requested by the other provinces. Be that as it may, it did indicate that it was not satisfied with this act as it stood. If that province does not put this act into effect, as it has a right to do, there will be no law in that province in so far as extra-provincial undertakings are concerned, and that goes for any other province that does not want to take advantage of this enabling legislation.
But I cannot see that any harm will befall anyone. Supposing for instance, there is a trucking company that wants to move from Victoria to the Atlantic provinces, say from Vancouver to Halifax, Nova Scotia, and one province says it will not put this act into effect; the truck can still go through; it will not be operating illegally. It was agreed by all the provinces it would be a good thing to have clause 5 or a clause that would be in the nature of clause 5.
I must say that subject to one reservation, because I am sure the hon. member for Bow River will probably want to correct me. There were some misgivings on the part of Alberta, but they did come along and state they would be satisfied to accept that clause. They preferred another method, but rather than see the position of extra-provincial undertakings in the way it is now, they would much rather have this bill.

Well, I believe I have answered the four questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East, as I had them noted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I now quote briefly this statement from the Saskatchewan brief:
Until the S.M.T., (Eastern) Limited litigation-
That is the Winner case.
-began it seems to have been generally assumed that a motor vehicle, carrying freight or passengers was under the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of that province in which the vehicle happened to be situated at any given moment. In other words, no legal concept was considered to be involved other than property and civil rights in the province.
As my hon. friend knows, that comes within provincial jurisdiction. Then, the brief says:
It followed, therefore, that the legislative jurisdiction of a province over highways within the 83276-377J
Motor Vehicle Transport boundaries of the province was complete in the matter of use thereof by interprovincial or international motor carriers.
Therefore the province, as this correctly states, up until that time had been dealing with intra-provincial transport, which was and still is wholly within that provincial jurisdiction, and had also been dealing with interprovincial transport between provinces, and also with the international transport, such as that involved in the Winner case which came from a location in Maine and went up through two Canadian provinces.
Until the privy council said it was illegal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite right -until the privy council said it was illegal. And perhaps if I read one or two short extracts from the privy council judgment, we might illuminate another point that has been giving my hon. friend difficulty. Their Lordships said this:
The province has indeed authority over its own roads but that authority is a limited one and does not entitle it to interfere with connecting undertakings-
A connecting undertaking such as the Winner movement.
It must be remembered that it is the undertaking, not the roads which comes within the jurisdiction of the dominion, but legislation which denies the use of provincial roads to such an undertaking or sterilizes the undertaking itself is an interference with the prerogative of the dominion.
Whatever provisions or regulations a province may prescribe with regard to its roads it must not prevent or restrict interprovincial traffic.
As Their Lordships have indicated, this does not in any way prevent what is, in essence, traffic regulations, but the provisions contained in the local statutes and regulations must be confined to such matters as traffic regulations.
Then, Their Lordships go on to say that whether the legislation in question in any case is, in pith and substance, traffic regulation or whether it is an interference with interprovincial traffic, must be decided on the facts of the case before the court. In the Winner case, they held it was an interference with or sterilization of interprovincial traffic.
Now, that being so, upon the privy council rendering its decision in the Winner case, the problem which arose was as to what was to be done with regard to that regulation of interprovincial traffic which up until that time had been provided by the province. They had the organization, the staff and everything else that the dominion did not have. The bill that is now before the house enunciates and provides for the bringing into effect of the principle that the officials in the provincial transport boards shall, in effect,

Motor Vehicle Transport continue to provide, under federal jurisdiction and authority, that control over interprovincial and international traffic, which up until the present time they had exercised, as it would appear from the Winner judgment perhaps wrongfully, under provincial authority. And that is the reason why this Bill 474 authorizes the provincial boards to carry along that control over interprovincial traffic which the hon. member for Vancouver East says is just the same as it is at the present time.
Now, so far as a province in which this act has not been proclaimed is concerned, any interprovincial traffic which flows through that province cannot be interfered with or sterilized; for the only way in which a province, after the Winner case was decided, can control, regulate or license interprovincial traffic, is under the federal authority given by this present bill, particularly sections 3 and 4.
If my hon. friend will examine the section before him he will see it says, simply, that a provincial motor transport board shall under its terms regulate, and shall have power to grant licences to interprovincial traffic. And the provincial boards will have that power by virtue of the action of this parliament exercising federal jurisdiction to clothe the provincial motor transport board's personnel with such powers.
My hon. friend asks how that can be done. Again I would refer him to this excellent Saskatchewan brief which says, as is obvious-
-that the only way in which this problem can be dealt with, whether as in this bill or even if the dominion government assumed control itself over interprovincial and international traffic, would be to correlate its efforts in this field with the efforts which the provinces at the same time would be putting forth to control intraprovincial traffic.
So no matter what legal alternative is adopted by this parliament, we still have to have the co-operative approach. And you cannot get a better example of the co-operative approach than the bill now before the house. The Saskatchewan brief puts it in this way:
The co-operative approach proposed depends upon the method of overcoming the constitutional division of legislative competence. It seems clear on constitutional grounds that the outright delegation of authority from the federal government to provincial governments or vice versa is out of the question.
That is to say, parliament cannot clothe a provincial legislature with the power to pass an act which the provincial legislature itself has not the power to pass, under the British North America Act. Then the brief goes on in these terms:
It seems equally clear however that-

As the Minister of Transport explained a moment ago, in line with this decision in the Prince Edward Island marketing board case- -a provincial board may receive the authority of the parliament of Canada to carry out certain functions within the jurisdiction of that parliament. This power is not impaired by the fact that it has also received the authority of a provincial legislature to carry out certain functions within the jurisdiction of that legislature.
In other words, when a provincial legislature has clothed the persons in a provincial board with power to deal with intra-provincial motor traffic, it is then quite within the power of this parliament to come along and pass this bill, and say to the members of that board, "You shall also have federal authority under this bill to control interprovincial traffic."

That may have the effect of extending the present jurisdictional gap until next February or March in many cases. Motor Vehicle Transport ministers that they were saying that enabling provincial legislation is necessary in such cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, I did not say that.
If I misapprehended the minister's argument I would wish that it be cleared up for the record now, because the point is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In my last statement a few moments ago I thought I made the position as clear as I could make it, and that is, that the federal parliament can clothe any group of people that it chooses with powers to exercise authority under this legislation. It may be that with some eight or nine provinces coming under this arrangement and with the provincial legislation doubtless varying to some extent, from one province to another, by reason of the nature of the type of board created under a certain provincial statute, clarifying provincial legislation might be needed to make it clear that that precise board could accept authority granted to it by federal legislation. Apart from some difficulty of that sort that may occur in legislation that I have not even seen, I do not think there is any difficulty presented at all by this parliament clothing certain persons with authority which they may exercise under this bill.

One further question:	I
understood the minister to say that this bill had been submitted to the dominion-provincial conference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:

Extra-provincial traffic; all
right. As 1 understand clauses 3 and 4, this legislation will completely legalize all their operations. Am I right there?

That, Mr. Chairman, is exactly the way I understood it, except that I do not see where the interprovincial board comes in in those provinces. The minister has not made that clear. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it is very simple. An interprovincial undertaking crosses provincial boundaries from time to time. When it crosses the interprovincial boundary between British Columbia and Alberta going west it comes into the province of British Columbia and its activities as an interprovincial undertaking in British Columbia will by virtue of this bill be under the control of the members of the provincial board acting under federal authority.
Where is that in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will look at clause 3 he will see it says:
(1)	Where in any province a licence is by the law of the province required for the operation of a local undertaking, no person shall operate an extra-provincial undertaking in that province unless he holds a licence issued under the authority of this act.
(2)	The provincial transport board in each province may in its discretion issue a licence to a person to operate an extra-provincial undertaking into or through the province upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if the extra-provincial undertaking operated in the province were a local undertaking.
I think it is very clear. As long as they are in that province their activities are under the control of that board acting under federal authority.
What I understand my hon. friend from Vancouver East is now driving at is this. In view of the fact that a provincial undertaking may extend through seven or eight provinces, how can a number of separate boards, each having authority to deal only within its own area, control this operation; that is, their
IMr. Garson.]

operations through seven or eight provinces. Well, Mr. Chairman, the answer to that is found in arrangements which have now been in existence in Canada for some considerable period of time under which, by reciprocal arrangements between those various provincial authorities, licensing is provided for the undertaking through all of those provinces for fees that will be perhaps 100 per cent in the home province of the undertaking and for less than 100 per cent in the other provinces and in some cases American states, in consideration of those provinces and states extending the same kind of an arrangement in respect of such interprovincial undertakings as are located in those other provinces as their home provinces. These reciprocal arrangements exist by virtue of the same kind of interprovincial co-operation as we are now trying to perpetuate by dominion-provincial co-operation. This is the way and the only way in a federal state in which it is possible to secure that over-all regulation of interprovincial motor traffic in all of the provinces concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I go back to my question of half an hour ago. We have had quite a long answer, but part of my question is still unanswered.
