speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought I had answered that question when I quoted rather extensively from the judgment of the privy council in the Winner case. It seems to me that the position there is this: Once the Winner case is decided in the way in which it was decided, no provincial board can regulate an interprovincial undertaking except under federal authority. Therefore, if this act be not proclaimed in a certain province there will not be in that province any board that can do anything more than provide traffic regulations, weights, and so on with respect to interprovincial undertakings and, as I understand it, there will be no board in that province which will have the power to prevent an interprovincial undertaking from going through that province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, during the time in which that truck is going through that province it is not under any jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is under possible federal jurisdiction which is not in esse by reason of

the tact that the relevant federal statute has not been proclaimed to be in effect in that province.
Let us stop there. I do not quite understand. Let us speak in English.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: "In esse" means "in being".
I do not know what that term means.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It means "in being".

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has put us on the track. If there is one province or more which does not come under this act when passed by the house and a truck passes through that province, then I take it that, in accordance with the decision of the privy council, it will then be the responsibility of the federal government and that they will convey that truck through on their regulations. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend's question is asked as being relevant to the bill which is now before us. Under the circumstances he names I do not think I can add anything to the answer I gave a moment ago to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If this bill becomes law and it is not proclaimed in a province, then an interprovincial undertaking can take its trucks through that province, and providing it complies with the rules of the road, traffic regulations, weights, and so on, it cannot be denied ingress or egress or passage through the province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this bill was to fill a vacuum which now exists, and even after the bill is passed if there are provinces which do not wish to have this bill proclaimed with respect to their area there will still be a vacuum to that extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend calls that a vacuum-

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, and I do not want to hold up the passage of this clause, but I wish to be quite clear about this. I do not think there is a vacuum. I understood the minister to say that if a province does not come in on this agreement after the act is passed then, regardless of this vacuum, if a truck complies with the rules of the road then that truck cannot be denied ingress or egress or passage through that province. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask if the same thing applies to buses. For example, in the past buses coming from
Motor Vehicle Transport Alberta through Saskatchewan, particularly in the case of the Greyhound line buses from Calgary to Saskatoon, had to discharge their passengers as soon as they reached the Saskatchewan border, and the passengers had to board a different bus. Does that still apply?
Clause 2 (a) covers that point.

What is the
answer?
I thought I answered that this is covered by clause 2 (a), which covers both passengers and goods.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 agreed to.
On clause 3-Operating licence.

Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting for some time to deal with some of the points I wish to make, though I might add that some have been anticipated in the earlier discussion which, I thought, should have taken place under this clause. I would like to follow up in some detail the question of whether this scheme will in fact succeed, whether it is sound judicially, and whether if it is to succeed it does not require concurring provincial legislation.
As I understand it, the legal basis on which the department has proceeded in drafting this legislation is the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case in which it was held that while parliament has no authority to clothe a provincial legislature with any of its jurisdiction, it has nevertheless the authority to delegate to a board which may have been set up under provincial legislation the administrative power which the federal government would have had the right to confer on its own board, had it created such a board.
But I suggest that that case cannot be taken as deciding anything beyond what it decided on the basis of the facts on which it so decided. I suggest there is a fundamental difference between the facts in that case with respect to the marketing of potatoes, and the facts which would be present in a case of a highway or public utilities board seeking to exercise control over the operation of a truck outside its borders or, alternatively, one which had come into its borders from outside under a licence granted by an authority outside its borders.
In the Prince Edward Island potato case the marketing board itself which was given authority to exercise the federal parliament's administrative jurisdiction was not using the

Motor Vehicle Transport roads of another province. The only persons who would be using the roads of another province would be using them as individuals and therefore that province would naturally have complete and exclusive jurisdiction over them, whereas what the government is purporting to do under clause 3 is to allow one province to say how a person shall be allowed and who shall be allowed to use the road from another province. I submit there is a fundamental difference in the factual basis of the two situations so that the Prince Edward Island potato case can be of no application to this situation where you are trying to give one province the authority to exercise, with respect to the use of the road from another province, the authority which is vested only in the federal government.
I would like to hear from either minister as to how they feel the case of P.E.I. Marketing Board v. H. B. Willis Inc. is applicable as general authority for the present legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In reply to my hon. friend's question, I would point out that if he will examine the bill he will see that clause 3 of the draft bill requires an operating certificate, if the provincial laws require an operating certificate for a local undertaking. Under subclause 2 the provincial board is authorized to issue such a certificate and in doing so the provincial board is required to follow provincial rules applicable to the issuing of a provincial certificate. Provincial legislation of this character applied to local undertakings would be constitutional.
Now, the reply to my hon. friend's question, I think, is this, that parliament can confer authority on provincial boards, as was decided in the case I quoted, namely the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case, and parliament can adopt provincial rules by reference. In the various statutes there are several examples of this, as my hon. friend knows. They are not confined to the Prince Edward Island case by any means. As I would point out, this practice differs from delegation. Parliament is not attempting to confer upon the legislature of any province jurisdiction to enact laws that the provinces themselves would not have the power to enact under the British North America Act. I see my hon. friend nodding his head in assent. That was the position that I took earlier. Parliament here is simply saying that the rules that a provincial legislature has validly enacted within the ambit of its powers in relation to a subject matter over which it has jurisdiction shall be rules applicable in relation to a subject matter


over which parliament has jurisdiction. Recognizing the point or the purported point of the remarks which my hon. friend made a moment ago, I am endeavouring to state the precise reason why this proposed bill is intra vires of parliament.

I agree with the proposition
the minister has put forward as to the scheme of this bill. But the point that I made-and which the minister has not dealt with-is that the judicial basis upon which the government says that this bill will stand up is the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not exclusively.

On what other basis, then?
What other authority is there for it? That is the case which established clearly and beyond any doubt that the federal government had the authority to delegate to a board set up by a provincial authority the administrative authority which the federal government might otherwise have conferred upon its own board. That is my point. I am not questioning the decision. That case is obviously the final declaration of the law.
What I am pointing out is that that case cannot be taken as authority for any proposition which goes beyond the facts upon which that case was decided. What was done there was to give the Prince Edward Island potato marketing board authority to regulate the marketing of Prince Edward Island potatoes in areas where otherwise the Prince Edward Island board would not have had any authority. It was with respect to produce originating within that province and over which therefore, initially at any rate, that province had jurisdiction; the jurisdiction of that province over produce originating within it was extended outside the province by the delegation.
What you are doing here, however, is the exact reverse. The facts are completely inverted as between the two cases. Here this legislation seeks to delegate to a provincial board authority to make regulations with respect to an undertaking which originates outside the province and is seeking to go into the province. In other words, this bill seeks to give, say, to the Alberta board power to make regulations governing the passenger or freight-carrying activities of a British Columbia corporation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Within the province of Alberta.
Within the borders of Alberta.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: Why not?

This is the exact inverse of what was done in the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case where the authority of the Prince Edward Island board was in respect of potatoes originating in Prince Edward Island, and where they were allowed, as it were, to follow them outside of their borders. They were not given authority to take something coming from outside, under the order in council that was passed, and to make with respect to it provincial regulations which they would not otherwise have had authority to make. Therefore the facts of the two situations are completely different.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With great respect may I say that I think my hon. friend, in the remarks he has just made, has overlooked the fact that all that this bill purports to do is to clothe the provincial board with federal powers in respect of those matters which are taking place within the province in which the board acts. That is all it purports to do. Because an undertaking is interprovincial and because it passes through British Columbia and Saskatchewan and Manitoba does not give the Alberta board power over it in respect of those things that take place in connection with it outside of Alberta. But, in relation to those things which took place in Alberta, this bill is simply saying that the rules that a provincial legislature has validly enacted in relation to a subject matter over which it has jurisdiction shall be the rules applicable in respect of a subject matter over which parliament has jurisdiction. The board is dealing in the one case with intraprovincial motor transport operations and in the other case with interprovincial operations.

Perhaps the minister and I just will not be able to come to a mutual understanding of the point I am trying to make, so I leave that one for the time being and come to another one.
The question has been raised already as to the necessity for the provincial legislatures' enacting concurrent legislation to authorize their boards to accept jurisdiction. So far I do not think we have had a clear answer on that point. But again, going back to the statement of principle which I do not think the minister could controvert-and I do not think he would want to do so-namely that the basis of this legislation is the Prince Edward Island potato marketing board case, again I say that that case cannot be taken as authority for a proposition with respect to facts which are entirely different. It is only authority for a proposition where the facts are similar. In that case the Prince Edward Island legislature had passed legislation authorizing their
Motor Vehicle Transport marketing board to accept jurisdiction and administrative authority which might be conferred upon it by the dominion government under its concurrent legislation. Chief Justice Rinfret, in his judgment, referred specifically to that feature of the case, as will be found at page 398 of the Supreme Court Reports of 1952. His judgment with respect to that portion of it, which held that the Prince Edward Island board was properly authorized to make regulations under the dominion statute, was in part most clearly based upon the fact that that board had been authorized by its own legislature to accept that jurisdiction. Any other proposition, of course, would lead to an absurd result which I am quite sure the government, if it gives it any consideration, would not seriously put forward, namely that a board set up by a province for one purpose and with no thought that it should step in for another purpose, might suddenly be told by the dominion government: We want you to act for us in this particular respect and capacity. That proposition, of course, would be perfectly absurd. I am sure that the government would not seriously put it forward for a moment.
I should therefore like to hear further from the minister as to what provinces have agreed to enact concurrent legislation and what happens if they do not enact it; and in the meantime, I should like to hear what answer he gives to the proposition already put forward by the hon. member for Eglin-ton, in the absence of that concurrent legislation. In many provinces it cannot possibly take place now until the session of the legislature next spring. What happens to the gap in the meantime to which reference has already been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have answered this same question three times already, I think, and I really despair-
The minister has talked all around it; he has not answered it.
The minister has not come to grips with the points that have already been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.

Does the minister agree that the Prince Edward Island case was decided on the basis that there was passed in that province legislation authorizing their board to accept jurisdiction conferred under the dominion statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is just playing with shadows. Does my hon. friend entertain such a low opinion of the provincial

Motor Vehicle Transport governments of Canada that he thinks they would send their representatives-in many cases their premiers and their attorneys general-down here for a two-day conference and then would be unwilling to take any steps that might be necessary to make effective this bill which they approved? Does he think that? And if he does not think that, what is the sense of these points which he has been raising?

I am not going to be put off by any ridiculous approach. I asked the minister a question which I assumed, perhaps wrongly, it was within his competence as Minister of Justice to answer. Will the minister answer the question?
He has half a dozen times.
He has not answered it yet.
He has.

Does the minister know? Has he read the Prince Edward Island potato marketing board case recently? Does he know? Has he got any information whether it was based on the fact that there existed enabling legislation within that province?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
No, Mr. Chairman, not until the Minister of Justice shows the usual courtesy which is customarily expected from ministers, and answers a serious question in a serious manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will leave it to members of the house whether I have exhibited the usual courtesy.
Too much.
Has the Minister of Justice got any opinion on the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have expressed it four or five times.
The minister has not dealt with that question at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Now, Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, if I may say so, that remark of my hon. friend is completely inaccurate. I have answered this specific question two or three times already, and I think there is a limit to the number of times that one should have to answer the same question.

I challenge the minister to examine the record at any stage and find where he answered the question which I asked him, namely, whether he does not agree that the decision in the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case, on which this legislation is based-
[Mr. Garson.l
Partially.
-was based in large part on the ground that enabling legislation already existed in that province. I challenge the minister to show where he has answered that question at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend has not been very attentive to the discussion this evening.
Wait a moment. I have the floor at the moment.
You asked for an answer and he is giving it to you.
Read it in Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Let him go on and talk as much as he likes.

The minister has, it is true, sought on a number of occasions to evade dealing directly with the question whether or not it will be necessary for the provinces to pass enabling legislation, but he has not answered the question as to the basis on which this case was decided and whether or not, therefore, it will be necessary for similar legislation to be enacted elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I recall it, in my previous remarks at quite an early stage I referred to the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case as being authority for a rather elementary principle in constitutional law which I am sure the hon. member for Kamloops will not challenge, namely, that the federal parliament can confer federal authority and powers upon a board which is also exercising provincial powers. That is the only purpose for which I cited that case, and that is a sound statement of law for which that case is authority. I did not go into any of these details and technicalities my hon. friend is now bringing up. It may very well be that upon the facts involved in the potato marketing board case in Prince Edward Island it was necessary there, and that the provincial authorities did enact that that board should receive from the provincial legislature the authority to receive federal powers.
But I said in reply to the hon. member for Eglinton that, without having seen the relevant provincial legislation of any of the eight provinces involved with regard to motor transport, I could not commit myself offhand to an opinion, in respect of legislation that I have never seen, as to whether it would be necessary, in the light of that provincial legislation, for these provincial legislatures now to pass further provincial legislation authorizing the boards set up under their existing legislation to receive federal powers. My hon. friend himself is a lawyer. How much further could I spell out the answer

to a question of that sort? How does he expect me to give an opinion with regard to eight or nine provincial transport laws that, unfortunately, I have not seen? Would he do it?
Oh, gladly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And what would he charge his client for an opinion of that sort?

The minister has of course gone a great deal further in what he has said now than he did previously in answer to my question with respect to the effect of the Prince Edward Island potato marketing case. He has stated an opinion for which I personally would not pay anything because he has attributed to the case an authority which it does not contain in citing its finding, as he says, that the dominion government can empower any provincial board to exercise authority which would be otherwise reserved to the dominion parliament. I submit to him that case is no authority whatsoever for that proposition. It is on this point that I have been endeavouring to draw him into an intelligent discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On a question of privilege, my hon. friend is again attributing to me remarks that I did not make, but I have no objection to that because Hansard will record what I said and it will record what he said that I said, which is a very different thing.

I am trying to get to a basis of sensible understanding with the minister and I am not trying to say that he said things he did not say. I understood him to say, in explanation of the proposition he now puts forward, that the Prince Edward Island case established what he himself called an elemental constitutional proposition, namely, that the dominion parliament might clothe a provincial board with authority to exercise administrative functions within the purview of the dominion parliament. Is that not a fair summary of what the minister said? Does he now wish to challenge it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, so stated it is quite
correct.
That is, as I recall it, what I said the minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh no, it is not.
All right, we will proceed on the basis of what we have now got before us. I say that the minister in making that statement-
You are getting slower every day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Get down to some facts.
Motor Vehicle Transport

-has incorrectly interpreted this case because the Prince Edward Island case was decided on the basis of a set of facts which was that the Prince Edward Island legislature had previously conferred upon this board authority to accept delegated dominion administration. It is authority for no other proposition and it cannot, I submit, be cited as authority for the vague general proposition that the dominion government can run around the country giving provincial boards set up for one purpose authority to do things for which they were never set up. No court would of course agree with the interpretation of this decision which the Minister of Justice has just made, I submit, for the very reason that it obviously was not intended to lay down the proposition that boards set up for one purpose by the provinces could be clothed with authority for an entirely different purpose by the dominion unless the provinces themselves authorized the boards to accept that authority.
Eight attorneys general have already agreed on this point.

We have been trying to find that out, and the minister has sought to answer that question by indirection. He has said: Do you suppose that the attorneys general would come down here and agree to this proposed legislation if they did not intend to see to it that their boards had the authority to carry it out? No, I give the attorneys general credit for rather more intelligence than the Minister of Justice-
Oh, oh!

-does. What we are asking him, and I think we are entitled to an answer, is in how many provinces does there exist that enabling legislation? If the ministers do not know why do they not say so and save all this discussion?

May I try to clear up one point. I did not, during the course of the conference, discuss this subject matter with all of the attorneys general. It would not be accurate nor true were I to say that. But I discussed it with a number of them, and all agreed that this was the way in which to pass the legislation. I refer particularly to one attorney general whom I met out in the western provinces. He asked me how we were going to do this, weeks before the conference took place. I indicated to him how we proposed to do it. He said, that is the only way in which it can be done. He said he had given this very careful consideration and had come to the conclusion the only way in which the dominion could clothe the provinces with control was by virtue of a statute which

Motor Vehicle Transport would enable the provincial boards to do interprovincially what they were doing intra-provincially.
The draft bill which was circulated, and which was studied, is the result not of the Minister of Justice or of the Minister of Transport, but is the result of the conference of premiers in some cases and attorneys general in other cases, with their legal advisers who were there. They all came to the conclusion that this was the way in which to deal with it. Well, are we going to deal with this problem or are we not? If we are not going to deal with it-
I wish you would just answer the question, that is all.

I know, but if we are going to deal with it, this is the method by which to do it.
My hon. friend has asked several questions in an attempt to differentiate between the Prince Edward Island potato case and this case. It may be so that the Prince Edward Island potato case is not entirely on all fours with this case, but that does not derogate from the fact that this, in the opinion of all those perhaps some 20 lawyers who were there, is good law.

I agree that if it is going to be done by delegating authority to the provincial boards this is the only way to do it. I thought I had made it clear that the basis of this decision, and the subject of my inquiry, was that it appears that concurrent provincial legislation is also necessary. The very simple point I am asking is: Are the ministers in a position to tell us how many provinces have the necessary concurrent legislation; and, in the case of those that have not, what is to happen in the meantime about this apparent gap which will occur?

How many provinces have concurrent legislation? Perhaps I could reply in this way. At the conference the provincial ministers of highways were there, the attorneys general were there, and they must know whether or not they have concurrent legislation in the province. I would think, from what I know of the position, that the vast majority of the provinces have concurrent legislation. I know they have it in Ontario and Quebec. I think they have it in most of the maritime provinces. I believe they have it in Manitoba, but I have not got the statutes before me; I do not know.
I could say that had this particular problem been of the magnitude my hon. friend feels it is, rightly or wrongly, it would have been raised then because surely those provinces who consented to the principle of this draft bill must have known whether or not


they had concurrent legislation. Notwithstanding that, the attorneys general felt they could go along with this bill.

We in the federal parliament are concerned with the matter of interprovincial highway traffic control. I would have thought that the minister would feel he should be in a position to satisfy the federal parliament on the question: When this bill is passed, how many provinces will be in a position to apply it? That is what we want to know. Is this measure going to produce the desired results? I agree that this is the only approach if the solution is to give authority to the provinces, but what we want to know here, and I think are entitled to know, is when the measure is enacted how many provinces will be in a position to bring it into effect and have that control.

I think that is a fair question. How many provinces will be able to apply this provision? I believe all the provinces will be able to apply it. I feel that the provinces will put it into effect, save and except one. I speak now of the nine provinces. There was one province, Newfoundland, that was not represented at the conference, for obvious reasons, and that province will not need to put it into effect. From the conversations I have had with representatives of the provinces, from the correspondence that has come from each and every one of the provinces, save one, I feel this act will be put into effect as soon as it is passed.
It would have been a lot simpler if the minister had answered first, instead of having his colleague confuse the situation.

May I turn to another point raised by section 3? Section 3 provides:
... no person shall operate an extra-provincial undertaking In that province unless he holds a licence issued under the authority of this act.
It further provides that:
The provincial transport board in each province may in its discretion issue a licence to a person to operate an extra-provincial undertaking-
We have not spelled out here anywhere in the act any detailed provisions about the licence. This is the sum total of the provisions of the statute in regard to the issuance of a licence. I am sure the minister is aware that in the provinces which have entered into the field of controlling intra-provincial highway transport traffic, there are many types of licences. There are licences pertaining to common carriers; there are licences pertaining to contract carriers, and there are various types of each of those depending upon the type of route over which the licensee is to operate.

This section speaks only of a licence. The form of the licence is not prescribed. There is nothing here to indicate whether there is to be only one type of licence applicable to all types of highway transport. We have the whole question raised as to whether the operators of buses are to receive the same licences as operators of trucks. What about class A operators on the highways? What about class B operators on the country roads? What about class C contract carriers?

There are hundreds in
Ontario, as my hon. friend knows.
I believe the classes now run up to H.
There are many types in Ontario.

There are many types for public commercial vehicles, and then we have passenger vehicles as well. It struck me as being very strange that this bill lacked provision to cover this point. It simply speaks about a licence. The form is not prescribed nor-and this is an equally important point-Mr. Chairman, does this section lay down the terms upon which a licence is to be granted. If you look at its provisions it simply says that the provincial transport board may, in its discretion, issue a licence. What is to be the meaning of that expression? What rules are to guide the provincial transport boards in the issuance of licences under the authority that is purported to be conferred upon them by this act?
The minister is aware that these provincial transport boards operate for the purpose of controlling the operations of public commercial vehicles and public passenger vehicles. They do so under the provisions of statutes which, in practically every case, direct that the licence be issued on proof of public convenience and necessity. There have been some interesting decisions, both in this country and the United States, upon what constitutes public convenience and necessity. There certainly has not been, on the part of provincial boards, any uniform interpretation of the meaning of those words, but at least they have some value in giving direction to the provincial transport board as to the grounds upon which they should proceed in dealing with applications. In the legislation now before us there is not one circumstance or rule to guide the provincial transport boards in dealing with applications for extra-provincial licences. This seems to me to be an extraordinary situation. It is left entirely to the discretion of the provincial transport board-an unfettered discretion. It
Motor Vehicle Transport seems to me that the house ought to give very careful consideration to language as broad in scope as this, conferring jurisdiction upon a provincial board without making the slightest attempt to lay down rules to guide that provincial board in dealing with such applications.
These are the questions which occur to me. What kind of licence is to be issued? What is to be the form of the licence? Who is to lay it down? Upon what rules are provincial transport boards to proceed in entertaining applications for licences for interprovincial operations?

I think the language set out in clauses 3 and 4 is meant to leave with the provincial boards the discretion, in so far as all the questions my hon. friend from Eglinton has raised, if I understand him correctly.
Let us take the province of Ontario as an example. My hon. friend is perhaps more familiar with that province, as I am. He knows that there are perhaps hundreds-I might be mistaken in that-but there are certainly-
They run from A to H, inclusive.

Oh, far more than that. The attorney general in the province as well as the minister of highways said that there were countless numbers of licences granted by the Ontario railway municipal board to these various groups.
But there are not that many classes. The classes are set out in the regulations under the act. If my memory serves me correctly they run from A to H.

Well, there are several classes, and several classifications, too, in respect of any licence granted by the board under the general rule of public convenience and necessity.
The provincial boards have had a great deal of experience in dealing with these applications for franchises, licences, permits, or whatever you call them-because different provinces call them by different names. They have had a lot of experience. We felt we should not tie provincial boards down to any particular kind of licence, or class or classification, but that they should be authorized to deal with extra-provincial applications in the same way, in the same method and under the same rules and conditions as they were dealing with intra-provincial applications.
That is the way the provinces wanted it. I remember very well the discussion having to do with Ontario, and that is certainly the way the attorney general and the minister

Motor Vehicle Transport of highways in Ontario wanted it. They did not want it any other way, either. If this were to be amended the attorney general in Ontario would be the first to protest, and to protest vigorously. Clauses 3 and 4 covered the situation and suited Ontario best. There was some doubt about it at first; but after a full discussion we came to the conclusion that this was the method by which to authorize these provincial boards to deal with extraprovincial licences.

Do I understand the minister to say that the words "upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if the extra-provincial undertaking operated in the province were a local undertaking" import the rules as to the jurisdiction in these cases that would apply under provincial legislation? In other words, are we to understand that these words have the effect of importing the rule that the applicant must make out a case of public convenience and necessity before he establishes the right to a licence under this act?

If that is the position in the province, I would think that that will be the position hereafter. Certainly, if I understand correctly the rules in Ontario, a carrier must prove public convenience and necessity before he can obtain a franchise. And if this bill goes through he would still have to prove it.

I am not at all satisfied that that is the result of this clause. I can understand the desire of the attorney general in Ontario to have applications of this kind dealt with in the same way as applications now coming before the Ontario municipal board for licences to operate intra-provincial highway transport. But I am not at all sure that that follows from the language used here. The words used are, "upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner". It does not say, "subject to the same conditions or upon the same grounds".
This is an important question, because there is only one rule under the legislation of Ontario to guide the municipal board as to whether it should reject or allow an application. An application must prove public convenience and necessity. It is open to grave doubt whether any of these sections import that ground of jurisdiction or that condition of jurisdiction of the municipal board. I think it is open to grave doubt, because the words "like terms and conditions" apply, I should think, to the terms of the licences; and the words "in like manner" apply to the procedure before the board.
The minister knows that an application today is made to the department of highways.

The department of highways refers the application to the municipal board, and there are certain forms that are completed, and certain proofs filed. Then the municipal board directs that the application be put on the list for public hearing.
It seems to me that the incorporation of that proceeding exhausts the significance of the expression "in the like manner". Therefore I come back to the original point which, it seems to me, is one of substance, that even if this clause is passed, we have not said that the municipal board, as in the case of an application for an intra-provincial licence, must confine itself to a case where an applicant has established proof of public convenience and necessity.

I feel, and I still think, that these words mean exactly what they say. The words "upon the like terms and conditions and in the like manner as if the extraprovincial undertaking operated in the province were a local undertaking" mean exactly what they say, and would authorize the extra-provincial movement in the same manner as the board authorizes intraprovincial movement. It was difficult to use other language.
My hon. friend has said: Why not tie the language down to meet a particular position? Well, it is a fact that certain provinces do not require proof of public convenience and necessity. Other provinces deal with the carriers in a way different from Ontario. And it is because of those various reasons that this broad and general language was used.
All I can do is accept the language of the draftsmen. The draftsmen have been some time doing this-draftsmen from the eight or nine provinces who were present. And it was drafted on the advice of the Department of Justice. So I have to accept it as meaning exactly what it says.

I take it this will give to the provincial authorities power to do that which was the whole basis of the Winner case, in that a provincial board here would have the authority to refuse the operator of a bus or truck line the right to pick up and set down passengers within a province, even although the main operation of the truck or bus operator was across the province and between two other provinces. I take it from the wording of this clause that it is sufficiently wide open to permit a provincial board to make such a prohibition, if it desired to do so.

Let me answer my hon. friend's question in this way. The provincial board can license an extra-provincial carrier

or refuse to license an extra-provincial carrier in the same manner as the provincial board is now licensing or refusing to license an interprovincial carrier.

Then that establishes it quite clearly. I agree with the minister in that interpretation, but I should like to have it clear that in the same way that the province of New Brunswick had the power to prevent a carrier in that case from picking up and putting down passengers within the province-that is, from picking up and putting down the same passenger within the province of New Brunswick on its way through-any board now would have the power to prohibit that from being done. I think that raises the question as to what steps are going to be taken by the federal authority to bring the provinces together to seek to bring about uniformity in matters of that kind to prevent the province that would have a natural inclination to do so from favouring their own commercial carriers, and thus to seek, by the refusal of licences to carriers from outside the province, to put traffic in the way of their own commercial undertakings that might lead to great difficulties in the development of trans-Canada trucking systems and bus systems. Admittedly this is a possibility I am speaking of, but I think it is a possibility that we in the federal parliament would have in mind. I should like to hear from the minister whether, after this act has been in operation for some time, any steps are in contemplation for working up a uniformity in truckers' regulations in respect to licensing.

As to the extra-provincial undertaking that exists now and that is operating from one end of the country to the other, if the provincial boards choose to give them a franchise and authorize them to go into each province, then those extra-provincial carriers can certainly pick up and set down-
If they get a licence.

As to those that are now already operating, then, I suppose it would be within the discretion of the province to say no. If the province of Ontario, for instance, feels that there are far too many, or that there are a sufficient number of extra-provincial carriers, it can turn the application down; and if it does, well, the extra-provincial carrier is just out of luck.
My hon. friend raises a good point when he asks, well, what procedure is in mind? If this legislation goes through we shall soon find out how it operates. The understanding at the conference was that if this did not
Motor Vehicle Transport operate satisfactorily there was no difficulty about amending the act or perhaps finding a better solution than this. This was certainly the best solution that could be found at the time. If it is not satisfactory, parliament sits for eight months of the year-parliament will sit I do not know when, but certainly within the next few months-and I think we shall have an opportunity of looking at this again. But the act should be given a chance to operate to see if it will not be successful. We think it will, and believe the provinces do also.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 4-Tariffs and tolls.

I have a point on clause 4. The minister is no doubt aware that while some provinces have legislation clothing the lieutenant governor in council in some cases, or provincial boards in others, with the power to require the publication of tariffs and tolls and to enforce them, nevertheless in many cases that power has not been exercised, and there is no effective legislation in force on the point.
As long as that situation continues I presume there will be no room for the application of clause 4. But let us assume now that the situation changes and the provinces, or a sufficient number of them for the purpose of the discussion, do decide to require the publication of tariffs and tolls and adherence to them. Let us take the case of the trucker who starts off from, we shall say, Alberta, and passes through Saskatchewan and Manitoba and then swings down into the United States, enters Ontario, goes through Ontario and Quebec, crosses over into United States territory, goes through New Brunswick and ends up in Nova Scotia. Now, I presume that in those cases-we are dealing with through freight-any carrier is going to be quoting a toll on the through shipment from Alberta to Nova Scotia. Will the minister indicate how a clause like this is going to work out in a case of that kind where you have a toll established on a through movement that may go through, let us say, eight provinces and cross the international border four times. How are we going to deal with that? Are we going to have every one of the provincial boards in every one of those eight provinces passing on a through toll that has nothing to do with local shipments? This is a matter of toll on a through shipment from Alberta to Nova Scotia which is quoted as a single toll by the carrier to the shipper.

I do not anticipate any great difficulty there because the truckers are operating now from one end of the country

Motor Vehicle Transport to the other and they are operating by virtue of what are known as reciprocal agreements.

The minister has not followed my point. That may be all very well now when the provinces are not applying it because either in some cases they have not the legislation or in other cases they have not proclaimed the legislation that gives them the right to require the publication of and the adherence to the tariffs. But the case I am pointing out to the minister is where the provinces have exercised that power and the publication of tolls is required and the adherence thereto is enforced.
Well, the publication of the toll is required in certain provinces. It is required in the province of Ontario, and is adhered to. My understanding is that it is. If I am wrong'-[DOT]
There is authority in the act, but the power given under the act has not been used.
Well, I have been under the impression that it was. Certainly that was the impression that we got at the conference.
It has been in the act for some years.

Again I repeat, I do not anticipate any difficulty there. It is being done now. Truckers are today quoting rates from one end of Canada to the other for movement of goods and all this does is to enable the provincial board to fix the rate. So far as the publication of the tariff and the toll is concerned, will that not be a matter for the provinces? And if the position is as I said earlier, that there are a number of interprovincial agreements or reciprocal agreements as to tariffs and as to tolls, then I cannot anticipate any difficulty. The provinces certainly did not anticipate any difficulty when they discussed it here at the conference.

I may not have made my point as clear to the minister as I should have. It may be natural for him to wish to simplify a situation of this kind, but I am putting to him a case which is rather different from the situation that exists today. I am wondering how a series of provincial boards, in the case I am putting, the provincial boards of eight provinces, are going to deal with the question of passing on a through toll on a through shipment from Alberta to Nova Scotia, going through eight provinces and crossing the international boundary four times. You are going to have eight provincial boards required to pass upon one toll on a through shipment that has to move from Alberta to Nova Scotia. It seems to me

an extraordinary requirement. You are going to have a toll of that kind approved by eight provincial boards when the toll is a through one and it cannot be broken down to divide it into a portion of movement that is performed in a particular province.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 5-Exemption.

I had assumed that we would hear some explanation of the real purpose of clause 5. Nothing more has been said that would explain what amounts to a complete withdrawal of this power at any time the government should choose to exercise that authority.

Mr. Chairman, I should perhaps have dealt with that when I spoke earlier. The Leader of the Opposition seemed to be of the opinion that this was taking terrific powers and, in fact, the expression he used was that we were taking "extremely wide powers" under clause 5 of this bill. I will explain as best I can why these powers are necessary.
They are necessary in order to protect the position of certain provinces. They are necessary, for instance, if the province of New Brunswick sought at one time or another to prohibit the through traffic of interprovincial transportation into Nova Scotia say, from the province of Quebec or Ontario. The province of Nova Scotia insisted that a clause such as this would be necessary in order to protect them. The province of Ontario at first took the view that that was not so. But after the Minister of Justice had explained the meaning of the clause the province of Ontario then felt not only that such a clause was necessary, but that without it the act would not be operative.
Then we are, as my hon. friend knows, committed by international undertaking to the movement of trucking across certain highways such goods as were agreed under GATT. I have not before me the agreement which was reached, but under GATT there is a very definite agreement with reference to the transportation of goods along Canadian highways, and it was thought necessary to bring that to the attention of the conference. When it was brought to the attention of the conference it was agreed that such a clause should be inserted therein, with the exception to which I referred earlier.
Then there is the question of defence movements. It was assumed that at some time or other it would be necessary to move defence trucks across the provinces into the Northwest Territories and so forth, and it was felt necessary that this clause should be inserted.

After an explanation had been given by the federal authorities the provinces felt that this clause was a reasonable one to insert in the bill.

Mr. Chairman, it is still not at all clear how this would be exercised. The power given here is the power to exempt any person or the whole or any part of any extra-provincial undertaking, or any extraprovincial transport, from all or any of the provisions of this act.
The effect of that, no matter what the intention may be, is to make it possible for government by order in council to exclude from all the provincial regulations any highway transport throughout the whole of Canada. The fact that the government may not intend that, in no way limits that possibility. I am simply pointing out that powers are given and the government retains the power to take the whole of it away.
Now, when the Minister of Transport says that conceivably the province of New Brunswick might introduce some licensing regulations that would interfere with the movement across that province, I realize that he is merely using that by way of illustration. But when he uses this illustration he says in so many words that the provinces can have these powers as long as they are good boys, but that at any point when they are not good boys, in the opinion of the government here, the application of these provincial regulations will be withdrawn in that area in relation to any transport that may be designated by the government here.
Surely that is a wide power. Surely it is an undesignated power. And surely it is a power that negatives the rule of authority apparently conferred by this bill. I submit this is not the kind of power that should be contained in a bill of this kind, and I also submit that it is an extraordinary clause.
The very illustration given by the minister of the example of New Brunswick indicates just how unsatisfactory a situation could result from legislation of this kind. Now, I would ask the minister to go a little further so we can understand the position, and, again using New Brunswick as an illustration, give us an exact illustration of the kind of specific situation where he thinks the government might be called upon to act, and the kind of order in council he has in mind which might be passed under this particular clause.

I would answer the last part of my hon. friend's comment by saying that I hope it will not be necessary for the federal government to use the powers conferred under clause 5, and I hope it will not be necessary to pass any orders in council
Motor Vehicle Transport under clause 5. I do not think it is a question of the provinces being good boys. I think it is a question of protecting a certain position that they have taken. Take, for instance, the question of GATT, to which my hon. friend did not refer at all. We are committed by international agreement to allowing the transportation of certain goods extra-pro-vincially under certain circumstances. If we were to give that power away and dispense with clause 5 where would we be? We would certainly be in an untenable position with reference to that international agreement. We would be in the same kind of position with reference to our defence forces. We have simply put this in with the object of using it if the occasion arises, but I think the provinces realize that we have no intention of making any unnecessary or undue use of this clause, and in any event it would cover extra-provincial traffic and would in no way affect the internal movement within the provinces.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to labour this because I feel that, having regard to the responsibilities the government is assuming for introducing some legislation to fill a vacuum which has been created, and no matter how unsatisfactory it may be, it is just as well to deal with the legislation before us. I asked the minister to give us a specific illustration in relation to the province he mentioned, New Brunswick, and the answer he gave was that the government did not expect to use this power. That would be like the Minister of Justice saying, when asked under what circumstances capital punishment should be applied, that he could best answer that question by saying that the government hoped it would not be necessary to apply it. I do not think the Minister of Justice would do that, although he does give some rather circuitous answers on occasion.
The minister said that New Brunswick is an example of a situation where the government might have to act; but let us have a simple explanation of the kind of situation he means and what kind of order in council the government might have to pass.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of answering the last part of my hon. friend's question. I have already given him three reasons-

Yes, GATT, the movement of transports to the Pacific, and extra-provincial traffic; but none of these have anything to do with the simple question of getting things across New Brunswick from Nova Scotia.

I dealt with that originally. That was the first example I used, namely

Motor Vehicle Transport the example of New Brunswick; but apparently I did not make myself clear because my hon. friend comes back and asks me to deal with it again. The province of Nova Scotia took the position that if New Brunswick wished to prohibit traffic moving from Ontario or Quebec into the maritime provinces it could do so. The province of Nova Scotia felt that that would not be a fair position for it to be placed in, and it said, "All right, we will go along with this bill but on condition that someone has the right to protect our position in case another province in between tries to stop the movement of such traffic." Clause 5 was devised as being that kind of method whereby that province or even the province of New Brunswick might be protected against another province. I used that only as an example. The brief which was filed by the province of Nova Scotia at the time indicated that that was its main interest. Recently, not later than after the bill was introduced into the house, I received a communication from the attorney general of the province of Nova Scotia approving of this clause as now placed in the bill. Those are the three reasons I can think of and I have expanded on reason No. 1. I do not know that I can go any further.

Then may I ask the minister if this would be a correct interpretation of what he has just said. If the province of New Brunswick introduced regulations which, in the opinion of the government of Canada, had the effect of restricting the movement of highway transport from Nova Scotia across New Brunswick, the government would then, under section 5, pass an order in council exempting from the application of the provincial regulations in New Brunswick highway transport moving from Nova Scotia through the province of New Brunswick?
No, Mr. Chairman; I said no such thing.

Unless the minister means
exactly that, his statement means nothing. We have no information of any kind as to what the real purpose of this section is.

speechtext:
Shall clause 5
carry?

Mr. Chairman, there is
another aspect of this matter-
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglinton wishes to make some remarks?
I think we are quite prepared to carry on.
Go ahead.
Speak for yourself.
Ten o'clock.

The minister was asked to indicate the kind of order in council which would be passed under this section if occasion arose. May I point out to him that the effect of the section is to permit the governor in council to exempt any person from any provincial provision in that case. That leaves that person in this area of vacuum in the law. There is in this legislation nothing that permits the order in council to name the conditions under which he may operate. If he is exempted from the provisions of this act, he is operating in a vacuum and there are no rules, federal or provincial, that restrict his operations in any respect whatsoever. It seems to me that that is an extraordinary situation. Is there no provision to which resort is to be had under the bill if exemption is given by order in council under this section with respect to all types of provincial regulation and control? It seems to be an extraordinary omission in a bill of this kind.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 5 carry?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does this clause not underline the fact that in reality the federal government is not giving these powers to the provinces but rather that the federal government is, of necessity, retaining powers which the courts have ruled are federal in character but is appointing these provincial boards as its agents to administer this authority in the various provinces? Having done that, by clause 5 of the bill the federal government is retaining this overriding authority in case any of these boards which are acting as its agents step out of line. Is that not the case?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall clause 5
carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. It is
perfectly obvious that we are not going to get a satisfactory explanation. As has been pointed out before, the government has permitted a vacuum to exist. That vacuum must be filled. The government now accept full responsibility for this measure. I would point out that section 5 simply permits the government to create a situation in which highway transport can run wild, and it will not even indicate to us how it proposes to deal with this matter, by what method or through what agency. There is nothing more that can be done but to let the government fulfil the undertaking that it has given to try to make this legislation work.

That is not the case, Mr. Chairman. I have now before me the brief presented at the conference by the province of Nova Scotia. It reads in part as follows:
There should be assurance that no one province can so affect extra-provincial highway transportation as to deprive any other province of extraprovincial highway transportation service and rights.
With respect to this second proposition, the situation under the privy council decision in the Winner case., we believe to be that the federal government has jurisdiction with respect to and responsibility for legislation relating to extra-provincial highway transportation. Some measure of retention of this jurisdiction and this responsibility by the federal government is in our view necessary.
That is why we put that in. I repeat what I said earlier, namely that the province of Ontario objected to this clause 5. But after the Minister of Justice and the attorney general for Nova Scotia had explained their position, the attorney general for Ontario said that of course the federal government should have this clause. Both he-that is the attorney general-and the minister of public highways for the province of Ontario subscribed fully to this clause in the bill.

I realize that it permits the governor in council to exempt from the provisions of the act so as to place in that area which we have called a vacuum today persons engaged in interprovincial and international highway operations.
This section might have been described as the section to perpetuate the vacuum so far as and whenever this government desires.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 5 carry?

Clause agreed to.
On clause 6-Penalties.
I have a question to ask on clause 6, Mr. Chairman. Who will be responsible for the enforcement of the provisions of the act and of licences issued under it?
It is ten minutes after ten.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Seeing that the authority of the provincial boards will be exercised under this act and will also be exercised under the authority of the provincial statutes with regard to intra-provincial operations, I think it necessarily follows that they would see to any prosecutions that would be necessary.

It is more than a question of prosecutions; it is a question of enforcement in a broad sense. From the answer given by the Minister of Justice, are we to take it that once this legislation is passed the federal government assumes no responsibility
Motor Vehicle Transport whatever for the enforcement of its provisions and of licences that might be issued in pursuance of its terms?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think perhaps, if my hon. friend would permit me to do so, it might be better to put it this way. There are in existence-and there have been for some years past-provincial boards which have been up to the present time and are now exercising jurisdiction over both intra-provincial and interprovincial motor transport. The federal authority, following the Winner case, has no such administrative body. The purpose of this bill is to leave both intraprovincial motor transport and interprovincial motor transport to be licensed, authorized, controlled and administered by the provincial boards. The only exception to that procedure, of course, is section 5 which, as the minister himself says, we hope we shall never have to invoke.
Carried.
Mr. Chairman, the minister has used a great many words-
Ten o'clock.

-which have no relation whatever to the question I put to him. I think there is a fundamental misconception here.
The provincial boards are not enforcement bodies. They are semi-judicial bodies which hear applications and determine when certificates of public convenience and necessity should issue. Then the possessor of such a certificate makes application to the department of highways and, if other requirements are satisfied, he obtains his licence. When it comes to the matter of enforcement, those provincial transport boards do not accept responsibility, that is to say with regard to whether there is compliance on the highway with the terms of the licence. Very often these licences are issued with limitations and conditions attached to them. If the Minister of Transport is correct in his interpretation of section 3, then presumably some of these licences issued with respect to international and interprovincial highway transports will contain similar conditions. Who is going to see to it that these conditions are fulfilled? Who is going to be responsible for them? Is the federal authority going to accept any responsibility for enforcement in situations of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend knows perfectly well that under the existing arrangements in all of the provinces the existing administrative authority looks after the licensing. The checking on the road is done by the provincial police forces, where they have provincial police forces. In those

Motor Vehicle Transport provinces that have a police agreement with the federal government under which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police discharge provincial police functions, the mounted police enforce the regulations in the same way as the provincial police, and the attorneys general of the provinces carry on any prosecutions that may be necessary. That arrangement will simply continue. Certainly there would not be much sense in continuing all the existing provincial enforcement bodies which have to be paid for by the taxpayers and have the federal government set up in addition an elaborate duplicate enforcement authority for which the taxpayers would also have to pay. I think my hon. friend's question answers itself.

If the question admits of a simple answer, I would be obliged if the minister would say so, that the federal government is not going to assume any responsibility in connection with enforcement but is proposing to leave that to the provincial authorities. If that is the case it would be the simplest thing in the world for the minister to say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I said that just a few moments ago. I said that would be the case unless it were necessary to invoke section 5 in which event we might be involved in a somewhat limited way.
But not otherwise? The minister nods his head.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-Proclamation in a province.
Is the minister in a position to say with respect to which provinces at the present time it is intended to proclaim this act?
It is not intended to proclaim this act unless the provinces indicate they want it passed, and as far as I know all of the provinces want this legislation with the exception of two.
It will not be proclaimed unless the province itself actually invites proclamation? Is that the situation?
From the correspondence I have in my hands now I think it would be possible to proclaim it in eight of the ten provinces.
But it will not actually be proclaimed until a definite request is made from the provinces? Is that the situation?

I think it can be taken that the request has already been made, not only at the conference but since, and I would take


it that request is sufficient. However, if it is thought that another request should be made that could be made.

I am simply seeking to
establish the basis on which it is to be done. Perhaps I can take it from the minister's answer that the federal government will be in a position to proclaim it with respect to all the provinces except two unless the minister receives a further communication from any one or more that they do not want it.
That would certainly be my recommendation to the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Before the last clause of the bill is carried I should like to say a brief word. In its excellent chapter entitled "National Transportation Policy" the Turgeon commission said a good many important things back in 1951, but they are summed up in this one sentence:
It is of course permitted to hope that the provinces will some day agree to co-operate with the federal authority in the carrying out of a common policy of co-ordination.
I express the hope, Mr. Chairman, in line with the view I expressed earlier that this bill be regarded as on a trial and error basis, that this legislation will not stand in the way of the eventual realization of that hope.
Mr. Chairman, I would draw to your attention that it is now ten o'clock and I ask you to call it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then the bill to repeal the National Physical Fitness Act, then consideration of the amendments made to the Criminal Code by the Senate, then the bill to which first reading was given this morning, namely, an act to amend the Criminal Code (race meetings). Then we will move to go into supply and take the departments of trade and commerce, transport, secretary of state and veterans affairs.

Mr. Speaker, could I ask now when we may expect to have some information about the Municipal Grants Act and the Judges Act?
Business of the House

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And the War Veterans Allowance Act?

I understand that notice of a resolution for the introduction of the amendment to the Judges Act will be in Votes and Proceedings of today and will be called as soon as it gets on the order paper. I was discussing the Municipal Grants Act with the Minister of Finance this afternoon and he will be making a statement on it at a very early time.
It being eighteen minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, June 15, 1954 Mr. Knowles: By leave.
